# How to Play This Book

> *"The road is long and the map is old, but every traveler starts at the same milestone: the one under their own feet."*
> — Viator Fortuitus, A Bard's Record

> ##### What This Book Is
> **Zelda DnD is a tabletop roleplaying game set in Hyrule.** You play it out loud, around a table, with dice. Everything that happens is described rather than displayed.
>
> You need **three to six people** and somewhere to sit. One of them is the **Dungeon Master**, who describes the world, plays every creature in it, and decides what happens when the dice land. Everyone else plays one hero, and speaks and acts as that person.
>
> A session usually runs **three to four hours**, and a campaign is as many sessions as the group wants. You will need dice, something to write on, and the 2014 D&D Player's Handbook alongside this book.
>
> If you have never done this before, read pages 4 through 9 in order. By the end of them you will know enough to build a character and take a turn, and page 6 shows you exactly what a turn sounds like.

This chapter is for anyone who has not played Dungeons & Dragons before, anyone who has not played a Zelda game before, or anyone who wants to know exactly which rules this book changes and which it leaves alone. Experienced players who want only the differences can skip to **Resources at a Glance** and the two glossaries at the end of this chapter.

---

## What Edition This Book Uses

**Zelda DnD is built for the 2014 edition of Dungeons & Dragons, 5th Edition.** You will need access to those core rules to play. This book supplies the races, classes, backgrounds, feats, spells, monsters, items, and setting; it does not reprint the core rules.

The most important rule in this book is this one:

> ##### The Default Rule
> If a rule is not described differently in this book, it works exactly as it does in the 2014 Player's Handbook. Ability scores, proficiency, advantage, conditions, resting, attunement, starting wealth, and everything else you already know are unchanged unless a section marked **New Rule** or **New Stat** says otherwise.

A short list of what this book does change, and where to read about it:

| Change | Replaces | Where |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Magic Points (MP)** | Spell slots | Magic System |
| **Stamina Points (SP)** | Nothing; new | Stamina System |
| **Called Shots** | Nothing; new | Stamina System |
| **Guard** | A shield's flat +2 AC | Items: Shields |
| **Weather Exhaustion** | Optional rules | Temperature |
| **Armor Sets** | Nothing; new | Items: Armor |


## What This Book Leaves Out on Purpose

- **There are no multiclassing rules.** A character in Zelda DnD advances in a single class. This keeps the custom resources, MP, SP, DPP, Energy, and Focus Points, from stacking in ways the classes were never balanced for.
- **There is no known-spells list.** This is deliberate and is explained under **Spellcasting Without a Spell List** below.
- **Attunement, carrying capacity, starting wealth, and downtime** follow the core rules unchanged.

---

## The Core Loop

Almost everything in this game resolves the same way.

**1. You say what your character does.** Not what you roll. What they do.

**2. The Dungeon Master decides whether it needs a roll.** Easy or impossible actions do not. Uncertain ones do.

**3. You roll a twenty-sided die and add a modifier.** The modifier comes from an ability score, plus your proficiency bonus if you are trained in what you are attempting.

**4. You compare the total to a target number.** Meet it or beat it and you succeed.

That target number has two names depending on what you are doing. When you attack a creature, it is that creature's **Armor Class (AC)**. When you do anything else, it is a **Difficulty Class (DC)** the DM sets, usually between 10 (routine) and 20 (very hard).

---

## Advantage and Disadvantage

When circumstances favor you, you roll two d20s and keep the higher. That is **advantage**. When circumstances work against you, you roll two and keep the lower. That is **disadvantage**.

They do not stack. Multiple sources of advantage still give you one roll of two dice, and if you have both advantage and disadvantage from any source, they cancel and you roll one die.

{{footnote Before You Begin | How to Play }}

{{pageNumber,auto}}

\page

## A Turn in Combat

When a fight starts, everyone rolls initiative (a Dexterity check) and acts in that order. Each round is six seconds of game time. On your turn you get all of the following, and you can use them in any order:

- **Movement** up to your speed, which you can break up around your other actions.
- **One action.** Attack, Cast a Spell, Dash, Disengage, Dodge, Help, Hide, Ready, Search, Use an Object.
- **One bonus action,** but only if some feature, spell, or item specifically grants you one. You do not get a bonus action by default.
- **Free interaction with one object.** Draw a weapon, open a door, pull a potion from your belt.

You also get **one reaction** per round, which you can take on anyone's turn. Opportunity attacks are the common one; in this book, shield parries and several class features also cost your reaction. Once you spend it, you have none until the start of your next turn.

---

## Resting

- A **short rest** is at least one hour of light activity. You recover Stamina Points and spend Hit Dice to heal.
- A **long rest** is at least eight hours. You recover all Hit Points, half your Hit Dice, all Magic Points, and all Stamina Points.

Zelda DnD adds one restriction that the core rules do not have. **You cannot take a short rest anywhere you are not actually safe.** Difficult terrain, extreme temperatures, active pursuit, and any area where Weather Exhaustion checks are in effect all prevent it. Finding shelter is a real decision in this game rather than a formality.

**A cleared room counts.** This rule is about the environment, not the postcode. A dungeon chamber the party has emptied and can hold, at ordinary temperature and off the patrol route, is a safe place to rest. Being underground is not itself a reason to refuse one.


## Resources at a Glance

Five different resources appear across the classes in this book. No character uses all five. Read the row for your class and ignore the rest.

{{classTable,frame
##### Character Resources
| Resource | Who Has It | Recovers | Spent On |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| **SP** Stamina Points | Every class | Short rest, if safe | Called shots, harsh terrain, class features |
| **MP** Magic Points | Every spellcasting class | Long rest | Casting spells |
| **DPP** Demonic Power Points | Blightbound only | Long rest | Cursed strikes and demon form |
| **Energy** | Veilblade only | 1 per turn; all on a rest | Special Attacks |
| **FP** Focus Points | Ranger only | Gained in combat | Ranger Techniques |
}}

The two you will see most often are **SP** and **MP**. SP is physical: everyone has it, and it is what lets a Sage who has never held a sword still vault a chasm or line up a precise strike. MP is magical: it replaces spell slots entirely, and a caster who runs out of MP has run out of magic until they sleep.

---

## Spellcasting Without a Spell List

This is the single largest departure from standard 5e, and it is intentional.

> ##### New Rule: No Known Spells
> Spellcasting classes in this book do not have a list of prepared or known spells. A caster may cast **any spell available to their class** at any time, provided they can pay its MP cost. There is no daily preparation step and no limit on how many different spells you use in a day.
>
> What limits a caster is the size of their MP pool, the escalating cost of repeating the same spell (see **Arcane Strain**), and the strain of casting high-level magic repeatedly (see **Arcane Saturation**). Those three rules together do the work that a known-spells list does in standard 5e.
>
> The one exception is a table that chooses to use the **spell slot alternative**. Every spellcasting class in this book prints a second class table using traditional 5e spell slots. A DM who prefers the standard system uses that table instead, and in that case the class prepares and knows spells exactly as its 5e counterpart would.

# An Example of Play

The fastest way to understand the rules above is to watch one round of combat play out. The character below is **The Wandering Hero** from the Example Builds in the next chapter: a 1st-level Hylian Adventurer on the Martial path, with STR 15 (+2), DEX 14 (+2), CON 13 (+1), a proficiency bonus of +2, leather armor, a longsword, a soldier's shield, and 2 Stamina Points.

---

**DM:** The Bokoblin at the top of the ridge has already seen you. It raises a horn to its mouth. Roll initiative.

**Player:** *(rolls a d20 and adds her Dexterity modifier of +2)* Fourteen.

**DM:** You go first. It is about twenty feet up a rocky slope, and the slope counts as difficult terrain.

**Player:** My speed is thirty, and difficult terrain costs double, so thirty feet of movement only carries me fifteen feet up. Can I spend Stamina to make up the difference?

**DM:** You can. That is what SP is for.

**Player:** I will spend 2 SP to cross ten feet of it as normal ground. Those ten feet cost ten movement instead of twenty, and the last ten feet at double cost make thirty exactly. So I am next to it, with no Stamina left. Then I take the Attack action with my longsword.

**DM:** Go ahead. Its Armor Class is 14.

\column

**Player:** *(rolls a d20)* Eleven, plus 2 for Strength and 2 for proficiency. Fifteen.

**DM:** Fifteen beats fourteen, so you hit. Roll damage.

**Player:** *(rolls a d8)* Six, plus 2 for Strength. Eight damage.

**DM:** The blade catches it across the ribs and the horn falls out of its hand. It is still standing, and it is angry. On its turn it swings a spiked club at you. *(rolls)* That is a sixteen against your AC.

**Player:** My AC is 13 from leather and Dexterity, plus 2 Guard from my shield, so 15. Sixteen hits.

**DM:** Four bludgeoning damage. Do you want to parry?

**Player:** A soldier's shield does not have the parry property, so I cannot. I will take the four.

---

**What just happened, rule by rule.** She rolled a d20 for initiative and acted first. She spent SP to ignore difficult terrain, which is a Zelda DnD rule and not a 5e one. She attacked by rolling a d20, adding her ability modifier and her proficiency bonus, and comparing the total to the target's AC. Her shield's **Guard** value added to her AC, which is how Guard works in this book. She could not use the parry reaction because that is a property of better shields, not of every shield.

Everything else in that exchange, the initiative order, the action economy, the damage roll, is standard 2014 5th Edition.

> ##### A Note for New Players
> You do not need to memorize any of this. The DM will tell you when to roll and what to add. The only thing worth remembering going in is the core loop: say what your character does, roll a d20, add your modifier, and compare it to a number. Everything else in this book is detail hanging off that one sentence.

{{footnote Before You Begin | Example of Play }}

{{pageNumber,auto}}

# Hyrule in Five Minutes

If you have never played a Zelda game, this is everything you need to sit down at the table. If you have, this is how this book uses the parts of the setting you already know.

---

## The Three Goddesses and the Triforce

Three Golden Goddesses made the world. **Din**, the goddess of Power, cultivated the land itself. **Nayru**, the goddess of Wisdom, gave the world its law and order. **Farore**, the goddess of Courage, created the living things that would uphold that law. Their colors are red, blue, and green, in that order, and those colors turn up on everything from temple tile to a Champion's armor.

When they departed for the heavens they left behind a symbol of their strength: the **Triforce**, three golden triangles that grant the wish of whoever touches them. Din's triangle is Power, Nayru's is Wisdom, Farore's is Courage.

The Triforce rests in the **Sacred Realm**, a holy world connected to Hyrule and also known as the Golden Land. The Sacred Realm reflects the heart of anyone who enters it. A pure heart makes it a paradise, and a wicked one turns it into a world of evil. The Sages and the Royal Family of Hyrule are its guardians, and nearly every catastrophe in Hyrule's history begins with someone trying to reach it who should not.

---

## The Kingdom

**Hyrule** is the kingdom the Triforce was left in, and the setting of this book. It has castles, farmland, ruins that are older than the castles, and stretches of wilderness where nothing has been mapped in a century. Its **Royal Family** descends from a line of princesses named Zelda, and the crest of that family, a stylized bird above three triangles, is stamped on shields, banners, and half the ruins in this book.


The other peoples of Hyrule have their own homelands and their own governments, and are not subjects of the crown so much as neighbors to it. The **Gerudo** hold the desert, the **Gorons** hold Death Mountain, the **Zora** hold the rivers and the domain at their source, the **Rito** hold the northern peaks, and the **Sheikah** serve the Royal Family from the shadows. All of them are playable, and the **Races of Hyrule** chapter covers each in full.

---

## The Recurring Enemy

Evil in Hyrule keeps coming back wearing the same face. **Ganon** is the name it takes most often: a Gerudo king turned Demon King who has sought the Triforce of Power in one era after another, and who has been sealed away and has returned more times than the histories agree on.

In the most recent age he returned as **Calamity Ganon**, an amorphous force rather than a person. Ten thousand years before that, the **Sheikah** had built a defense against exactly this: four mechanical wonders called the **Divine Beasts**, and an army of automatons called **Guardians**. Calamity Ganon corrupted the entire Guardian army with **Malice**, its own creeping, spreading substance, and turned them on the people who built them. Four skilled individuals called **Champions** were chosen to pilot the Divine Beasts. It did not go well for them.

This matters at the table because it is the source of most of the ruins, most of the ancient technology, and a good portion of the monsters in this book. Malice-corrupted enemies, Sheikah machinery, and Blights all trace back to it.

---

## Practical Matters

- **Rupees** are the currency, hexagonal gemstones whose color denotes value. The exact scale differs from age to age; this book uses the scale printed in the **Items** chapter.
- **Great Fairies** live in fountains scattered across the wilds. They heal the wounded, restore magic, and upgrade armor in exchange for materials, which is exactly how the armor upgrade rules in this book work.
- **Shrines, temples, and dungeons** are the structure most Zelda stories are built around: a self-contained place with a signature item inside it, a monster at the bottom, and a locked way forward that the item opens. The **DM Guide** has a full chapter on building them.

---

## What Era Is This?

Neither one nor all of them. **Zelda DnD is a composite Hyrule.** It does not sit on a single point of any official timeline, and it is not trying to. Deku and Kokiri, Twili and Zonai, Ocarina-era medallions and Wild-era armor sets are all in this book because they are all part of what Hyrule means, not because they coexisted in one age.

Use that however suits your table. Run the whole shelf at once and treat the older material as legend that turns out to be true. Or pick an era, keep what belongs to it, and let the rest sit in the Sacred Realm's long memory. The Factions chapter is written for exactly this: each faction is a set of motivations that hold across ages, with notes on how they shift depending on when you set your campaign.

Nothing in this book breaks if you cut a people, a relic, or a whole chapter out of it.

# Glossary: Dungeons & Dragons Terms

These terms belong to standard 5th Edition and are used throughout this book without further explanation.

**Ability Check.** A d20 roll plus an ability modifier, made to accomplish something uncertain. Add your proficiency bonus if you are proficient in the relevant skill.

**Ability Score.** One of six numbers rating your character: Strength, Dexterity, Constitution, Intelligence, Wisdom, Charisma. Each has a **modifier** derived from it, which is what you actually add to rolls.

**Action.** The main thing you do on your turn. You get one.

**Armor Class (AC).** How hard you are to hit. An attack roll must equal or exceed it.

**Attunement.** The bond required to use certain magic items. A character can be attuned to three items at once, and forming the bond takes a short rest.

**Bonus Action.** An extra, smaller action, available only when a feature specifically grants one.

**Cantrip.** A spell of no level that can be cast repeatedly. In this book a cantrip still costs 1 MP.

**Concentration.** The focus some spells require. You can concentrate on only one spell at a time, and taking damage forces a Constitution saving throw to keep it.

**Condition.** A defined status such as blinded, frightened, grappled, prone, or restrained, each with fixed rules.

**Difficulty Class (DC).** The target number for an ability check or saving throw.

\column

**Hit Dice.** The dice you spend on a short rest to heal. You have one per character level, of the size your class lists.

**Hit Points (HP).** How much damage you can take before dropping to 0.

**Initiative.** A Dexterity check made at the start of combat to set turn order.

**Long Rest.** Eight hours. Restores HP, MP, SP, and half your Hit Dice.

**Opportunity Attack.** A reaction attack you may make when a hostile creature leaves your reach.

**Proficiency Bonus.** A number based on character level, from +2 to +6, added to rolls you are trained for.

**Reaction.** One response per round, usable on anyone's turn, triggered by a specific event.

**Saving Throw.** A d20 roll made to resist something happening to you, rather than to make something happen.

**Short Rest.** One hour. In this book, only possible somewhere safe.

**Spell Save DC.** The DC a creature must beat to resist your spell. Equal to 8 + your proficiency bonus + your spellcasting ability modifier.

{{footnote Before You Begin | Glossary }}

{{pageNumber,auto}}

\page

# Glossary: Zelda DnD Terms

These terms are specific to this book. Each has a full entry in the chapter noted.

**Arcane Saturation.** Strain from casting expensive magic. Each spell costing 5 MP or more adds a level of it, and higher levels degrade your casting. *(Magic System)*

**Arcane Strain.** The escalating MP cost of casting the same spell repeatedly without casting a different one in between. *(Magic System)*

**Arcane Wounds.** What happens when a caster pushes past an empty MP pool. *(Magic System)*

**Blight.** A Malice-born champion of the Demon King, one bound to each of the four Divine Beasts. Several items in this book are written to counter them; the Bosses chapter does not yet provide their stat blocks. *(Items)*

**Called Shot.** Spending 2 SP before an attack to target a specific body part. On a hit, add an extra weapon damage die. Against a listed **weak point** it also triggers that creature's special effect. *(Stamina System)*

**Demonic Power Points (DPP).** The Blightbound's resource, spent on cursed strikes and demon form. *(Classes: Blightbound)*

**Energy.** The Veilblade's resource, spent on Special Attacks and regained every turn. *(Classes: Veilblade)*

**Focus Points (FP).** The Ranger's resource, earned during combat and spent on Ranger Techniques. *(Classes: Ranger)*

**Guard.** A shield's bonus to AC, replacing 5e's flat +2. Shields with the **parry** property can also spend a reaction to reduce damage. *(Items: Shields)*

\column

**Magic Points (MP).** The pool that replaces spell slots. Every spell has an MP cost, and any spell your class can cast is available to you if you can pay it. *(Magic System)*

**Malice.** The Demon King's corrupting substance. It animates ruins, turns machinery hostile, and marks a creature as his. *(Enemies)*

**Mantle.** A Champion's chosen goddess and the features that come with her. *(Classes: Champion)*

**Mask.** A form the Masked Wanderer can assume, granting the racial traits of another people. *(Classes: Masked Wanderer)*

**Overchanneling.** Spending extra MP as you cast to add damage dice or range. Replaces upcasting. *(Magic System)*

**Perfect Parry.** A parry with a shield that reduces the incoming damage to 0. Some shields and relics key an extra effect off one. *(Items)*

**Relic Save DC.** The DC for any relic that forces a saving throw and does not name one: 8 + your proficiency bonus + your highest ability modifier. *(Relics)*

**Set Bonus.** An extra effect granted for wearing all three pieces of an armor set, usually once each is upgraded twice. *(Items: Armor)*

**Soft Concentration.** A lighter form of concentration used by Sacred Songs, the Champion's Aura and the Interloper's Hex. It does not conflict with ordinary concentration, so you can hold one of each. *(Magic System)*

**Stamina Burn.** Ten minutes of meditation converting 2 SP into 1 MP, out of combat only. Stamina spent this way returns on a long rest, not a short one. *(Magic System)*

**Stamina Points (SP).** The universal physical resource. Every class has it. *(Stamina System)*

**Triforce Alignment.** The aspect of the Triforce a piece of magic reflects: Power, Wisdom, or Courage. It is flavor unless a feature says otherwise. *(Magic System)*

**Weak Point.** A specific vulnerability listed in a creature's stat block, exploitable with a called shot. Creatures without one use the Body Part Reference Table. *(Stamina System; DM Guide)*

**Weather Exhaustion.** Environmental exhaustion from heat, cold, or storms, resisted by the right armor set or the right meal. *(Temperature)*

{{footnote Before You Begin | Glossary }}

{{pageNumber,auto}}

# Character Creation

> *"Every hero begins the same way: uncertain, unarmed, and standing at a door that was not meant to stay closed. What matters is what you do when it opens."*
> — Viator Fortuitus, A Bard's Record

Creating a character for Zelda DnD is the first step in telling your story in Hyrule. This chapter walks you through the process step by step, whether you have never made a D&D character before or you are an experienced player learning what makes this homebrew different from standard 5e.

If you are new to D&D, read every section carefully. If you are experienced, pay particular attention to the sections marked **New Rule**. Those cover the mechanics and options that differ from the core rules.

By the end of this chapter you will have a character ready to play.

---

## What You Will Need

- This document
- A character sheet (standard 5e character sheet works with a few additions noted below)
- A set of polyhedral dice (d4, d6, d8, d10, d12, d20)
- A pencil

---

## Step 1: Choose a Race

Your race is the species your character belongs to. In Hyrule, the races are the peoples of this world, each with their own history, culture, and inborn abilities. Your race shapes your character before you have made a single other choice.

**The races of Hyrule are:**

| Race | Personality | Natural Strengths | Where They Are From |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| **Deku** | Curious, territorial, mischievous | Agility, nature magic, small size | Forests and wetlands |
| **Gerudo** | Proud, fierce, independent | Combat, desert survival, charisma | Gerudo Desert |
| **Goron** | Strong, loyal, jovial | Endurance, physical power, fire resistance | Death Mountain |
| **Hylian** | Adaptable, curious, ambitious | Versatility, extra skill, divine attunement | Hyrule Kingdom |
| **Kokiri** | Youthful, wary, bonded | Fey resilience, a fairy companion, woodcraft | Kokiri Forest and the Lost Woods |
| **Rito** | Swift, proud, observant | Flight, ranged combat, cold resistance | Hebra and coastal peaks |
| **Sheikah** | Disciplined, secretive, loyal | Stealth, ancient knowledge, speed | Kakariko Village and shadows |
| **Twili** | Enigmatic, perceptive, otherworldly | Twilight magic, illusion, shadow | The Twilight Realm |
| **Zonai** | Ancient, inventive, powerful | Construct mastery, elemental force | Ancient ruins and sky islands |
| **Zora** | Graceful, proud, devoted | Swimming, water magic, physical precision | Zora's Domain and waterways |

**How to choose:** Pick the race that excites you most as a personality, as a visual image, or as a set of abilities. Your race does not lock you into a particular class or role. A Goron Sage and a Goron Masked Wanderer both exist and both work. Ask yourself: *who is this person, and where do they come from?*

Once you choose, note your race's traits on your character sheet. Racial traits include your ability score bonuses, your size and speed, and any special abilities your race grants you. These are described in full in the **Races of Hyrule** chapter.

{{footnote Character Creation | Steps 1-2 }}

{{pageNumber,auto}}

\page

## Step 2: Choose a Class

Your class is your calling: the set of skills, training, and talents that define how your character interacts with the world. It determines your combat abilities, your access to magic, your Hit Points, and the resources you draw on to do remarkable things.

**The classes of Zelda DnD are:**

| Class | Role | Combat Style | Uses Magic? |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| **Adventurer** | Versatile hero | Weapon attacks, skills, and adaptability | Optional (Bard or Ranger path) |
| **Blightbound** | Dark power warrior | Cursed weapon strikes, eldritch power, dark contracts | Yes (Charisma) |
| **Champion** | Divine warrior | Holy weapon strikes, healing, divine authority | Yes (Charisma) |
| **Goddess Chanter** | Sacred support | Healing songs, divine blessings, harmonic power | Yes (Charisma) |
| **Interloper** | Twilight trickster | Illusion, enchantment, teleportation, subtlety | Yes (Intelligence) |
| **Masked Wanderer** | Shape-changing combatant | Martial prowess through mask-granted forms | No |
| **Ranger** | Nature hunter | Tracking, ranged precision, terrain mastery | Yes (Wisdom) |
| **Sage** | Elemental mage | Elemental spells, ancient knowledge, affinity mastery | Yes (Intelligence or Wisdom) |
| **Shaman** | Elemental conduit | Elemental marks, reactive spellcasting, spirit pacts | Yes (Wisdom) |
| **Veilblade** | Stealth striker | Precision attacks, shadows, tactical movement | No |

\column

**How to choose:** Think about what your character *does* in a fight, and what they do outside of one. If you want to solve problems through overwhelming force, look at Champion or Adventurer. If you want to manipulate and deceive, look at Interloper or Veilblade. If you want to call lightning and reshape the battlefield, look at Sage. If you want to channel the corruption of the Demon King into terrible power, look at Blightbound.

When you choose a class, record the following from its class entry:

- **Hit Die** (used to calculate Hit Points)
- **Proficiencies** (armor, weapons, tools, saving throws, skills)
- **Starting Equipment**
- **1st-level class features**
- **Your starting SP and MP** (see below)

---

### New Rule: Stamina Points (SP)

Every class in Zelda DnD begins with **Stamina Points (SP)**, a resource representing your character's physical endurance, focus, and ability to push past their normal limits. SP is recorded on your character sheet alongside your Hit Points.

**Every class starts with at least 2 SP at 1st level.** This amount increases as you level up, as shown in your class table.

**What you spend SP on:**
- **Called Shots:** Before making an attack, spend 2 SP to target a specific body part or weak point. On a hit, add one extra weapon damage die to the roll.
- **Difficult Terrain:** Spend 1 SP to move 5 feet through difficult terrain as if it were normal terrain.
- **Climbing, Swimming, or Crawling:** Spend 1 SP to treat 5 feet of these movement types as normal movement.
- **Class features:** Some class abilities cost SP to activate.

**Recovering SP:** SP fully recovers after a short rest *provided you can rest safely.* You cannot take a short rest while in difficult terrain, in extreme temperatures, during active combat or pursuit, or anywhere Weather Exhaustion checks are in effect. You need a sheltered, safe place to recover SP.

> **In play:** Stamina Points make every character, martial or magical, feel capable of heroic physical effort. Even a Sage who never swings a sword has SP to spend on dashing through rubble, shoving through deep snow, or lining up a called shot.

{{footnote Character Creation | Step 2 }}

{{pageNumber,auto}}

\page

### New Rule: Magic Points (MP)

If your class uses magic, it uses **Magic Points (MP)** rather than the spell slots found in standard 5e. MP is a single pool of magical energy you draw from each time you cast a spell.

**MP costs by spell level:**

| Spell Level | MP Cost |
|:--|:--|
| Cantrip | 1 MP |
| 1st level | 2 MP |
| 2nd level | 3 MP |
| 3rd level | 4 MP |
| 4th level | 5 MP |
| 5th level | 6 MP |
| 6th level | 7 MP |

Your class table shows your MP maximum at each level. At 1st level, most casters begin with 2 MP.

**Recovering MP:** Your MP fully recovers after a long rest. MP can also be partially recovered through **Stamina Burn**, a 10-minute meditation that converts 2 SP into 1 MP, usable outside combat in safe conditions. **Stamina spent this way is burned:** it returns on a long rest rather than a short one.

> **Key difference from standard 5e:** There are no spell slots and no spells known. You do not prepare spells at all. Any spell on your class's list is available to you at any time, and your MP pool is the only limit on which one you reach for. You can cast the same spell repeatedly, though doing so costs more each time (see **Arcane Strain**).

> **Escalating Spell Cost:** Casting the same spell again, without casting a different spell in between, raises its MP cost by 50 percent on the second cast and 100 percent on the third. To reset this, cast a different spell or skip a turn without casting. This discourages repetitive single-spell combat strategies. The full rule is in the Magic System chapter.

**Non-casters:** If your class does not use magic (Adventurer on a non-magic path, Masked Wanderer, Veilblade), you have no MP at 1st level. You may still use Stamina Burn if your class allows it.

{{footnote Character Creation | Step 2 }}

{{pageNumber,auto}}

\page

## Step 3: Determine Ability Scores

Your six ability scores measure your character's fundamental capabilities. They are **Strength, Dexterity, Constitution, Intelligence, Wisdom, and Charisma**. Almost everything you attempt in the game is shaped by these scores.

| Score | What It Governs |
|:--|:--|
| **Strength (STR)** | Physical power, carrying capacity, melee attacks |
| **Dexterity (DEX)** | Agility, reflexes, stealth, ranged attacks, AC without armor |
| **Constitution (CON)** | Health, stamina, endurance, concentration |
| **Intelligence (INT)** | Memory, reasoning, arcane knowledge |
| **Wisdom (WIS)** | Perception, intuition, willpower, nature attunement |
| **Charisma (CHA)** | Force of personality, social influence, divine connection |

**Generating your scores:** Use one of the following methods (your DM may specify which to use):

**Standard Array:** Assign these six numbers to your ability scores in any order: **15, 14, 13, 12, 10, 8.**

**Point Buy:** You have 27 points to spend. Scores cost the following:

| Score | Cost |
|:--|:--|
| 8 | 0 |
| 9 | 1 |
| 10 | 2 |
| 11 | 3 |
| 12 | 4 |
| 13 | 5 |
| 14 | 7 |
| 15 | 9 |

No score may be purchased above 15 before racial bonuses.

**Rolling:** Roll 4d6 and drop the lowest die. Record the total. Do this six times and assign the six results to your ability scores in any order.

**Applying Racial Bonuses:** After generating your scores, apply your race's ability score bonuses. For example, Hylians increase one ability score of their choice by 2 and another by 1.

**Calculating Modifiers:** Each score has a modifier used for most checks. Subtract 10 from the score, divide by 2, and round down.

| Score | Modifier |
|:--|:--|
| 8–9 | −1 |
| 10–11 | +0 |
| 12–13 | +1 |
| 14–15 | +2 |
| 16–17 | +3 |
| 18–19 | +4 |
| 20 | +5 |

**Which scores matter most for your class:**

| Class | Primary Score | Secondary Score |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Adventurer (martial) | STR or DEX | CON |
| Adventurer (Bard path) | CHA | DEX |
| Adventurer (Ranger path) | DEX or STR | WIS |
| Blightbound | CHA | CON |
| Champion | CHA | STR or CON |
| Goddess Chanter | CHA | WIS |
| Interloper | INT | DEX |
| Masked Wanderer | STR or DEX | CON |
| Ranger | DEX or STR | WIS |
| Sage | INT or WIS | CON |
| Shaman | WIS | CON |
| Veilblade | DEX | INT or STR |

{{footnote Character Creation | Step 3 }}

{{pageNumber,auto}}

\page

## Step 4: Describe Your Character

This step is where your character becomes a person rather than a collection of numbers.

### Background

Your background represents what your character did before adventuring: where they came from, what skills they developed, and what connections they carry into the world. Standard 5e backgrounds work in Hyrule. Some suggestions for Zelda-flavored interpretations:

| 5e Background | Hyrule Equivalent |
|:--|:--|
| Acolyte | Priest of a Golden Goddess, Sage initiate, Temple keeper |
| Soldier | Hylian Royal Guard, Sheikah warrior, Gerudo guardian |
| Criminal | Yiga Clan defector, black market runner, tomb robber |
| Folk Hero | Village defender, Goron champion, Zora legend |
| Noble | Hylian court member, Gerudo chieftain's heir, Zora royalty |
| Hermit | Wandering shrine hermit, exiled Sheikah, reclusive Sage |
| Outlander | Lost Woods survivor, Depths explorer, sky island wanderer |
| Guild Artisan | Armor smith, relic crafter, potion brewer |

Your background grants you two skill proficiencies, one or two tool or language proficiencies, a starting equipment package, and a background feature (a special benefit suited to your history).

### Personality and Motivation

Answer these questions and note the answers on your sheet:

**Personality Traits (choose two):** What are your character's defining habits, quirks, or attitudes? Traits should be specific. "I am brave" is too vague. "I always stop to examine unusual ruins, even when we're in a hurry" is specific and playable.

**Ideal:** What does your character believe in most deeply? This is the principle they would not compromise even under pressure. *"Every people of Hyrule deserves protection, not just the Hylians."* *"Power is earned, never inherited."*

**Bond:** Who or what does your character care about enough to take risks for? A person, a place, a sacred duty. *"I will find the sage who taught me, even if it means entering the Twilight Realm."*

**Flaw:** What is your character's weakness? A fear, a vice, a blind spot? *"I trust too easily, especially anyone who shows me kindness."* *"I cannot resist the call of an unexplored ruin."*


### Alignment

Alignment in Hyrule is a general moral compass rather than a rigid rule. The standard 5e alignment grid (Lawful/Neutral/Chaotic, Good/Neutral/Evil) applies, but you can think of it simply:

- **Good characters** protect others, even at cost to themselves.
- **Neutral characters** look after themselves and those close to them.
- **Evil characters** pursue power or survival at others' expense.

Most heroes in the Zelda tradition are Good or Neutral Good: courageous, protective, and on the side of light even when they work outside the rules.

---

## Step 5: Choose Equipment

Your class grants a set of starting equipment choices. Record what you take on your sheet, including armor type and any weapons with their damage dice.

### Armor and Armor Class (AC)

Your AC determines how hard you are to hit. Different armor types provide different base AC:

| Armor Type | Base AC | Notes |
|:--|:--|:--|
| No armor | 10 + DEX modifier | Monks and some unarmored builds apply differently |
| Light armor (Leather, Studded) | 11–12 + DEX modifier | — |
| Medium armor (Chain shirt, Scale, Breastplate) | 13–15 + DEX modifier (max +2) | — |
| Heavy armor (Chain mail, Splint, Plate) | 14–18 | No DEX bonus |
| Shield | + Guard value (+1 to +4) | Zelda DnD uses Guard instead of a flat +2 (see below) |

### New Rule: Shield Guard

In Zelda DnD, shields use a **Guard** value rather than a flat +2 AC bonus. A shield's Guard value is added to your AC while you wield it, exactly as the flat +2 would be. Shields in Hyrule range from a Bokoblin's slab of bark to the Hylian Shield of the royal family, so the bonus varies from +1 to +4.

Better shields also have the **parry** property. If your shield has it, you may additionally use your reaction, once per round, to reduce the damage of one melee attack that hits you by the shield's Guard value. A parry that reduces the damage to 0 is a **perfect parry**, which a few of the finest shields key an extra effect off.

The full shield table and the property definitions are in the **Items** chapter.

{{footnote Character Creation | Steps 4-5 }}

{{pageNumber,auto}}

\page

### New Rule: Weather Exhaustion and Equipment

Hyrule's extreme environments impose **Weather Exhaustion** on characters without the right gear or protection: Death Mountain's volcanic heat, Hebra's freezing snowfields, the Gerudo Desert's scorching sun.

When your character enters an extreme temperature environment, the DM will call for a **Weather Exhaustion check** (a Constitution saving throw). Failing this check grants one level of Weather Exhaustion, which carries increasingly severe penalties:

| Level | Effect |
|:--|:--|
| 1 | Disadvantage on **Perception checks** and **initiative rolls**. |
| 2 | Disadvantage on **all ability checks**. |
| 3 | Your speed is reduced by **10 feet**. At the start of each of your turns, choose **attack rolls or saving throws**. You have disadvantage on the chosen rolls until the start of your next turn. |
| 4 | Your speed is reduced by **20 feet**, and you **cannot gain advantage** on any d20 rolls. |

**Protective equipment:** Certain armor sets from the Zelda DnD equipment chapter provide immunity or resistance to specific Weather Exhaustion checks. When choosing your starting equipment, consider the environment your campaign will involve. A campaign set largely in the Gerudo Desert makes the **Desert Voe set** valuable early. A Hebra-based campaign makes the **Snowquill set** essential.

*Your DM can tell you what environments your campaign will frequently visit so you can plan your gear accordingly.*

\column

## Step 6: Record Final Numbers

Before you play, fill in the following on your character sheet:

**Hit Points (HP):** Take the maximum value of your Hit Die at 1st level and add your Constitution modifier. (Example: A Champion with a d10 Hit Die and +2 Constitution starts with 12 HP.)

**Proficiency Bonus:** At 1st level, this is **+2**. It applies to attack rolls, saving throws, and ability checks you are proficient in.

**Saving Throws:** Your class grants proficiency in two saving throws. For those, add your Proficiency Bonus to the relevant ability modifier. For others, use only the ability modifier.

**Initiative:** Equal to your Dexterity modifier. This determines your order in combat.

**Passive Perception:** 10 + your Wisdom modifier + Proficiency Bonus (if proficient in Perception). This is the number the DM uses to determine what you notice without actively searching.

**Stamina Points:** Record your class's starting SP from its class table.

**Magic Points:** If your class uses magic, record your starting MP from its class table. If not, write 0 or leave it blank.

**Your class spell list (if applicable):** You do not choose or record individual spells. Any spell on your class's list is available to you whenever you can pay its MP cost. Note where your class's list is printed so you can find it at the table, and see **No Known Spells** in the Magic System chapter.

**Languages:** All characters speak Common (Hylian) plus any additional languages granted by race or background.

---

## Step 7: Come Together

No character exists alone. Before your first session, talk with your fellow players and your DM about how your characters know each other, or how they come to meet. A few questions worth answering as a group:

- What brings your characters to the same place at the same time?
- Does anyone have a history with another character's background or homeland?
- Is there a shared goal that unites the group?

A party that has reasons to trust each other makes for better storytelling than a group of strangers who happen to fight in the same direction. Even one shared connection is enough to start with.

{{footnote Character Creation | Steps 6-7 }}

{{pageNumber,auto}}

\page

## Example Builds

These examples show what a finished character concept looks like. Each one is a rough archetype to start from. Change whatever you like.

---

### The Wandering Hero
*Classic Link archetype*
**Race:** Hylian | **Class:** Adventurer (Martial path) | **Background:** Folk Hero
**Key scores:** STR 15, DEX 14, CON 13
**Starting SP:** 2 | **MP:** None
**Concept:** A young Hylian with no memory of their past, carrying a sword they don't remember learning to use. Adaptable, observant, and unable to walk past an injustice. Speaks rarely and acts decisively.
**Starting equipment:** Longsword, soldier's shield (Guard +2), leather armor, explorer's pack, shortbow.

---

### The Divine Warrior
*Champion of the Goddesses*
**Race:** Hylian or Gerudo | **Class:** Champion (Mantle of Din) | **Background:** Soldier
**Key scores:** CHA 15, STR 14, CON 13
**Starting SP:** 2 | **MP:** None until 3rd level
**Concept:** A warrior chosen by a goddess who doesn't entirely understand why. Fierce in battle, loyal, and uneasy about what the goddess expects of her. Uses Charisma as her divine channel.

---

### The Sacred Singer
*Zelda / Sage of Song archetype*
**Race:** Hylian or Sheikah | **Class:** Goddess Chanter | **Background:** Acolyte
**Key scores:** CHA 15, WIS 14, DEX 12
**Starting SP:** 2 | **MP:** 6
**Concept:** A devoted priestess or temple singer whose faith has turned into real power. Heals allies, calls down divine judgment on enemies, and hears music in everything. Uses her ocarina as a spellcasting focus.

---

### The Twilight Infiltrator
*Sheik / shadow operative archetype*
**Race:** Sheikah or Twili | **Class:** Veilblade or Interloper | **Background:** Criminal (or Spy)
**Key scores:** DEX 15, INT 14, CON 12
**Starting SP:** 2 (Interloper) or 4 (Veilblade) | **MP:** 4 (Interloper); the Veilblade uses 3 Energy instead
**Concept:** A shadow operative who has learned to move between worlds, literally or figuratively. Gathers information, removes specific targets, and disappears before anyone asks questions. Their loyalty is complicated.

---

### The Stone-Fisted Sage
*Elemental power archetype*
**Race:** Goron or Zonai | **Class:** Sage (Earth Affinity) | **Background:** Hermit
**Key scores:** INT or WIS 15, CON 14, STR 12
**Starting SP:** 2 | **MP:** 9
**Concept:** A reclusive student of ancient elemental lore who has mastered the language of stone and force. Prefers to reshape the battlefield rather than stand in the center of it. Slow to anger, immovable when pushed.

\column

### The Desert Wind
*Gerudo warrior / drifter archetype*
**Race:** Gerudo | **Class:** Blightbound or Adventurer (Ranger path) | **Background:** Outlander
**Key scores:** CHA 15 (Blightbound) or DEX 15 (Adventurer), STR or CON 13
**Starting SP:** 2 | **MP:** 6 (Blightbound, as DPP); an Adventurer has no MP until 3rd level
**Concept:** A Gerudo who has wandered far from the desert, carrying either a dark pact made in desperation or a hunter's instinct honed by years in the waste. Self-sufficient, independent, and looking for someone she will not name.

---

## Quick Reference: Character Creation Checklist

- [ ] **Choose a Race.** Record racial traits and ability score bonuses.
- [ ] **Choose a Class.** Record Hit Die, proficiencies, features, starting SP and MP.
- [ ] **Determine Ability Scores.** Assign, apply racial bonuses, calculate modifiers.
- [ ] **Choose a Background.** Record skills, tools, languages, feature, and personality elements.
- [ ] **Choose Starting Equipment.** Record armor (and AC), weapons, and gear; note Weather Exhaustion protection if relevant.
- [ ] **Record Final Numbers.** HP, Proficiency Bonus, saving throws, Initiative, Passive Perception, SP, and MP.
- [ ] **Come Together.** Establish connections with the other characters before Session 1.

# Deku

*"The forest does not speak in words alone. It whispers through rustling leaves, drifting pollen, and the sharp crack of a seed striking bark. Those who learn to listen may find the Deku watching them long before they are ever seen."*

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; — *Viator Fortuitus*  
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; *A Bard's Record, Ch. 15 excerpt*

Small figures lurk among roots and branches, their wooden bodies blending into the forests and swamps they call home. To the untrained eye, a Deku may be mistaken for a knotted stump or a flowering shrub, until it moves, hops, or spits a hardened seed with startling speed.  

The Deku are a reclusive race of plant-like beings who dwell in dense forests and murky wetlands. Curious, territorial, and often mischievous, they guard their groves fiercely and treat outsiders with suspicion or opportunism depending on the individual. They are deeply attuned to nature, and use their innate magic to manipulate plants and evade danger. Though they are small, their agility and cunning make them formidable when provoked.

---

### Seeds of the Forest

Deku resemble small humanoid plants, their bodies composed of bark, vines, and leafy growth. Hollow, mask-like faces carved from living wood display exaggerated features: round eyes, wide mouths, and expressions that range from comical to unsettling. Their bodies are light and flexible, so they can leap, hop, and dart through dense terrain.

Though their forms vary slightly depending on habitat, most Deku stand between **2 and 4 feet tall**, with thin limbs and oversized heads. Many sprout leaves, flowers, or small branches that change with the seasons. Some Deku carefully cultivate their appearance, pruning themselves into pleasing shapes or adorning their bodies with colorful petals and seeds.

---

### Rooted in Time

Deku mature quickly, reaching adulthood within a decade. Unlike most mortal races, their lifespans are not fixed. **A Deku's life is tied to the health of its home grove.** Those who remain close to fertile forests and swamps may live for centuries, while Deku cut off from sunlight, water, or soil often wither and die prematurely.

Elder Deku remember events long faded from Hyrule's collective memory. When one of them talks about ancient kings, lost temples, or old calamities, it sounds like something they watched happen. This long memory makes them cautious and slow to trust, but also deeply respectful of tradition and natural cycles.

::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::

### Groves and Hierarchies

Deku society is structured around **groves**, each ruled by a powerful elder, often a **Deku King**, **Great Scrub**, or similarly titled figure. These leaders are believed to be partially fused with the forest itself, and they draw wisdom and authority from ancient roots and spirits.

Within a grove, Deku occupy specialized roles:  
- **Scouts and sentries** who watch from treetops  
- **Traders** who barter with outsiders  
- **Caretakers** who tend sacred plants and spirits  

Deku place great importance on **territory**. Trespassers are usually warned first: sometimes with riddles, sometimes with seedfire. Repeated offenses are met with hostility.

---

### Curiosity and Commerce

While many Deku are shy or defensive, others are surprisingly mercantile. These **Business Scrubs** wander trade routes, selling items at inflated prices and haggling relentlessly. To a Deku, commerce is a game as much as a livelihood, and a test of wit.

Adventuring Deku often leave their groves due to curiosity, exile, trade disputes, or visions granted by forest spirits. Some seek to heal dying woods, others to spread influence, and a few simply wish to see what lies beyond the trees.

{{imageMaskCorner29,--offsetX:52%,--offsetY:60%,--rotation:0
  ![](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AnthonyEllisDev/Zelda-DnD/main/images/DTCTlG2.png){top:0px,left:300px}
}}

{{imageMaskEdge4,--offset:3%,--rotation:270
  ![](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AnthonyEllisDev/Zelda-DnD/main/images/73Jhagl.png){top:10px,left:400px,height:500px}
}}

{{footnote Races | Deku }}

{{pageNumber,auto}}


\page

### Deku and the Other Races


**Hylians.** "Softskins with loud footsteps. Useful customers, unreliable guardians." Deku trade with Hylians but rarely trust them with forest secrets.

**Kokiri & Koroks.** Deku see these forest children as distant cousins, free-spirited and reckless, but worthy of protection.

**Gorons.** "Too loud. Too hot. Break too many trees." Relations are tense, though mutual respect can be earned.

**Zora.** Deku respect Zora waters, especially swamp-dwellers, but remain wary of flooding and pollution.

**Sheikah.** Deku distrust them deeply. Shadows do not belong in the forest.

---

### Deku Names

Deku names are often simple, descriptive, or based on sounds of nature. Many Deku change their names throughout their lives.

**Male Names:** Noko, Talo, Piku, Rishu, Maku, Dendo  
**Female Names:** Sera, Lili, Kanu, Vira, Miri, Palla  
**Neutral Names:** Sprig, Bud, Thorn, Root, Seed  
**Titles:** Scrub, Merchant, Sentry, Elder, King


### Deku Traits

Your Deku character has the following racial traits.

**Creature Type.** You are a Plant creature.

**Ability Score Increase.** Your Wisdom score increases by 1, and your Dexterity score increases by 1.

**Age.** Deku mature within a decade but can live for centuries, their lifespans tied to the health of their native groves.

**Alignment.** Most Deku tend toward neutral alignments. Their loyalty is to nature and territory rather than law or morality.

**Size.** Deku stand between 2 and 4 feet tall, with slender, bark-covered bodies. Your size is Small.

**Speed.** Your base walking speed is 25 feet.

**Languages.** You can speak, read, and write Common and Deku.

**Photosynthesis.** You do not need to eat food. If you spend at least 1 hour in direct sunlight during a long rest, you gain full sustenance. You also gain proficiency in the Nature skill.

**Deku Spit.** As a bonus action, you can spit a hardened seed as a ranged weapon attack (20/60 ft.). On a hit, it deals **1d6 bludgeoning damage**. This damage increases to **2d6 at 5th level**.

::::::::::::

**Deku Harden.** As a bonus action, you can harden your bark-like skin. For 1 minute, you gain a +2 bonus to your Armor Class. While hardened, your speed is reduced by 10 feet, and you cannot take the Dash action. Once you use this feature, you can't use it again until you finish a short or long rest. At 5th level, the AC bonus increases to +3.

**Deku Hop.** Your long jump and high jump distances are doubled.

**Subrace.** Three major subraces of Deku are found throughout Hyrule. Choose one of them.

---

#### Deku Scrub

The most common Deku, found guarding forests and swamps.

**Shrub Disguise.** You have advantage on Dexterity (Stealth) checks made in natural terrain.

**Forest Skulker.** You can attempt to hide even when only lightly obscured by foliage.

---

#### Mad Scrub

Aggressive and territorial Deku who rely on brute seedfire.

**Spit Specialist.** You have advantage on attack rolls made with your Deku Spit.

**Hardened Seeds.** Once per short rest, when you hit with Deku Spit, you can add an extra **1d6 bludgeoning damage**.

---

#### Business Scrub

Clever traders and wanderers, known for trickery and gliding petals.

**Silver Tongue.** You have advantage on Charisma (Persuasion) and Charisma (Deception) checks made to haggle or negotiate prices.

**Petal Glide.** Starting at **5th level**, you gain a flying speed of **30 feet** for up to 1 minute while not wearing medium or heavy armor. You can use this feature once per long rest.

---

# Gerudo

*"The desert does not forgive weakness. It tempers steel, hardens flesh, and burns away doubt. Those who endure its trials emerge stronger, or do not emerge at all."*

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; — *Viator Fortuitus*  
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; *A Bard's Record, Ch. 12 excerpt*

Beneath the blazing sun of the Gerudo Desert stand towering stone citadels and wind-carved fortresses, home to a people as fierce and unyielding as the sands themselves. The Gerudo are known across Hyrule as peerless warriors, master thieves, and survivors of a land that kills the careless. To face a Gerudo blade is to face generations of training.

---

### Daughters of the Desert

Gerudo are tall, broad-shouldered humanoids with dark or sun-bronzed skin, sharp features, and striking crimson or amber eyes. Their fiery red hair, worn long, braided, or bound in elaborate styles, is a point of cultural pride. Their movements are confident and purposeful, honed by a lifetime of combat training and desert survival.

Almost all Gerudo are born female. Once every hundred years, a single male Gerudo is said to be born, an event steeped in prophecy, fear, and legend. These rare births have shaped Gerudo history. They left scars on the culture and a lasting wariness of tyranny.

---

### Hard Lives, Harder Wills

Life in the Gerudo Desert is unforgiving. Scorching days, freezing nights, sandstorms, and scarce water ensure that only the strong endure. From a young age, Gerudo children are taught combat, endurance, and self-reliance. Weakness is not shamed, but it is not coddled either.

Gerudo mature quickly, reaching adulthood in their late teens, and most live less than a century. As a result, they value decisive action, personal honor, and living boldly. A Gerudo who hesitates may not live to see another dawn.

### Thieves, Merchants, Mercenaries

Though famed as warriors, Gerudo are also adept traders and thieves. Desert caravans are often Gerudo-run, guarded by skilled fighters and led by shrewd negotiators. In some lands, Gerudo are welcomed as elite mercenaries or bodyguards, so long as their terms are honored. A Gerudo's word is iron. Break it, and no desert will be far enough to hide.

::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::

### Law, Honor, and Tradition

Gerudo society is rigidly structured but not cruel. Leadership is traditionally held by a **Gerudo Chief**, chosen for strength, wisdom, and loyalty to the people. Beneath her are captains, warriors, artisans, and scouts. Every one of those roles is treated as essential to the tribe's survival.

The Gerudo Code governs all aspects of life, emphasizing:
- Strength through discipline  
- Loyalty to the tribe  
- Respect for proven skill  
- Vengeance for betrayal  

Exile is the harshest punishment a Gerudo can face. To be cast from the desert is to lose your name, your protection, and your people.

---

{{imageMaskCorner29,--offsetX:52%,--offsetY:50%,--rotation:0
  ![](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AnthonyEllisDev/Zelda-DnD/main/images/DTCTlG2.png){top:0px,left:300px}
}}

{{imageMaskEdge4,--offset:3%,--rotation:270
  ![](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AnthonyEllisDev/Zelda-DnD/main/images/mUYvYG7.png){top:0px,left:320px,height:600px}
}}

{{footnote Races | Gerudo }}

{{pageNumber,auto}}

\page

### Faith and Forbidden History

Gerudo religion is complex and cautious. They honor the Golden Goddesses, particularly Din, whose flame mirrors the desert's fury, but they also revere ancestral spirits and heroic matriarchs of old.

The shadow of **Ganondorf**, the Demon King born of the Gerudo, looms heavily over their history. Though he was defeated long ago, the wounds he left have not closed. Modern Gerudo watch for tyranny, corruption, and prophecy alike, and intend never to produce another Ganondorf.

---

### Gerudo and the Other Races

**Hylians.** "Soft, but adaptable." Gerudo respect Hylian persistence, though they find their politics frustrating.

**Sheikah.** Trusted allies, but never fully understood. Too many secrets.

**Gorons.** Kindred spirits in endurance and strength. Loud, but honorable.

**Zora.** Distant and elegant. Their waters are both coveted and feared.

**Rito.** Free spirits. Gerudo envy their freedom but distrust their detachment.

---

### Gerudo Names

Gerudo names are passed down through matriarchal lines and often carry meanings tied to storms, blades, or victory.

**Female Names:** Riju, Nabooru, Aveil, Buliara, Tali, Zira, Kasha, Sari  
**Titles:** Chief, Captain, Blademistress, Warden, Sandstrider

Male Gerudo, when born, are named according to ancient custom. Those names are often struck from the records after tragedy.

::::::::::::::::::::::::::

### Gerudo Traits

Your Gerudo character has the following racial traits.

**Creature Type.** You are a Humanoid.

**Ability Score Increase.** Your Charisma score increases by 2, and your Strength score increases by 1. Alternatively, you may increase two different ability scores by +1 each.

**Age.** Gerudo reach adulthood in their late teens and rarely live beyond 100 years.

**Alignment.** Most Gerudo tend toward lawful alignments, valuing order, tradition, and honor. Their personal morals vary widely.

**Size.** Gerudo are powerfully built, typically standing between 6 and 7 feet tall. Your size is Medium.

**Speed.** Your base walking speed is 30 feet.

**Languages.** You can speak, read, and write Common and Gerudo.

**Powerful Build.** You count as one size larger when determining your carrying capacity and the weight you can push, drag, or lift. You also gain proficiency in the Intimidation skill.

**Trained Fighters.** You have proficiency with scimitars, double-bladed scimitars, shortbows, and shields.

**Desert Temperature Endurance.** You have resistance to extreme heat and cold for the purposes of Weather Exhaustion checks. In addition, you can go twice as long without food and water as normal.

# Goron

*"Death Mountain earns its name. The air burns, the stone cracks, and the earth itself groans beneath your feet. Yet for the Gorons it is not a trial. It is home."*

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; — *Viator Fortuitus*  
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; *A Bard's Record, Ch. 20 excerpt*

High above the lowlands, where lava flows like rivers and ash clouds darken the sky, dwell the Gorons, living stonefolk whose laughter echoes through mountain halls. Massive, powerful, and unshakably loyal, Gorons endure conditions that would kill most other races within hours. To them, fire is warmth, rock is shelter, and hardship is simply another fact of life.

---

### Children of Stone and Flame

Gorons are large, round-bodied humanoids with skin resembling rock, stone, or hardened earth. Their bodies are dense and incredibly heavy for their size, with thick limbs, powerful torsos, and blunt, expressive features. Some Gorons have rocky growths, crystal deposits, or metallic veins embedded naturally in their skin, usually the same minerals found in their homeland.

Most Gorons stand between **6 and 10 feet tall**, though their hunched posture and barrel-shaped frames make them appear even larger. Despite their intimidating appearance, Gorons are famously expressive, quick to laugh, and prone to loud emotional displays.

---

### Slow Lives, Steady Hearts

Gorons mature far more slowly than most humanoids, reaching adulthood around their **eightieth year**. In return, they enjoy long lives, often exceeding **four centuries**. This longevity grants Gorons a patient, long-term perspective. Where others rush, Gorons endure.

They value **consistency, loyalty, and reliability** above all else. A promise made by a Goron is a promise carved in stone. Betrayal is nearly unthinkable, and forgiveness, while possible, is slow and deliberate.

:::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::

### Brotherhood of the Mountain

Goron society is built around **communal bonds** rather than strict hierarchy. Villages are typically governed by an elder or chieftain, chosen for wisdom and strength rather than bloodline. Decisions are often made collectively, after long discussion and sometimes shouting.

Family among Gorons is not strictly biological. Orphans are readily adopted, outsiders may be welcomed as "rock-brothers," and bonds forged through hardship are considered just as strong as blood.

Mining, stonecraft, and smithing are central to Goron culture, and so are feasting, contests of strength, and storytelling. Goron settlements are loud places, full of hammer strikes and the rumble of rolling bodies.

{{imageMaskCorner29,--offsetX:55%,--offsetY:45%,--rotation:0
  ![](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AnthonyEllisDev/Zelda-DnD/main/images/DTCTlG2.png){top:0px,left:300px}
}}

{{imageMaskEdge4,--offset:3%,--rotation:270
  ![](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AnthonyEllisDev/Zelda-DnD/main/images/aHhGMJa.png){top:-10px,left:300px,height:600px}
}}

{{imageMaskCorner20,--offsetX:-50%,--offsetY:-50%,--rotation:0
  ![](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AnthonyEllisDev/Zelda-DnD/main/images/qiuSnsF.png){top:775px,left:140px,height:20%}
}}

{{artist,bottom:80px,left:90px
##### Goron Crest
}}

{{footnote Races | Goron }}

{{pageNumber,auto}}

### Warriors, Miners, and Wanderers

Though not inherently warlike, Gorons are formidable fighters when roused. Their immense strength and resilience make them devastating shock troops, living battering rams that break enemy lines apart. Many Gorons favor heavy weapons, unarmed combat, or improvised tools over refined blades.

Some Gorons leave Death Mountain to trade, explore, or test themselves against the wider world. These wanderers are often driven by curiosity or a desire to prove their strength beyond the mountain's slopes.

---

### Faith Beneath the Mountain

Gorons honor the Golden Goddesses, particularly **Din**, whose fire they believe still burns within Death Mountain's heart. Many also revere mountain spirits, ancestral heroes, and the living will of the earth itself.

Volcanic eruptions, earthquakes, and rockslides are read as omens of change. A mountain that shifts is simply growing.

---

### Gorons and Other Races

**Hylians.** "Soft, but clever." Gorons respect Hylian ingenuity, though they worry constantly about their fragility.

**Gerudo.** "Strong sisters." Mutual respect forged through shared endurance of harsh lands.

**Zora.** "Slippery friends." Gorons appreciate Zora calmness but distrust deep water.

**Rito.** "Too light." Gorons struggle to understand a life spent in the air.

**Sheikah.** "Quiet ones." Gorons trust them, but find their secrecy uncomfortable.

---

### Goron Names

Goron names are typically short, rhythmic, and often end in hard consonants. Many include references to stone, heat, or strength.

**Names:** Daruk, Goron, Darmani, Yunobo, Torda, Gotis, Bludo, Rohan  
**Nicknames:** Rock-Brother, Stone-Fist, Boulder, Emberheart

---

### Goron Traits

Your Goron character has the following racial traits.

**Creature Type.** You are a Humanoid.

**Ability Score Increase.** Your Strength score increases by 2, and your Constitution score increases by 1.

**Age.** Gorons reach adulthood around 80 years of age and can live up to 400 years.

**Alignment.** Most Gorons tend toward neutral or lawful alignments. They value loyalty, honesty, and community over abstract ideals.

**Size.** Gorons are massive and powerfully built, typically standing between 6 and 10 feet tall. Your size is Medium.

**Speed.** Your base walking speed is 25 feet.


**Languages.** You can speak, read, and write Common and Goron.

**Powerful Build.** You count as one size larger when determining your carrying capacity and the weight you can push, drag, or lift.

**Fiery Endurance.** You have resistance to fire damage. In addition, you are immune to the effects of extreme heat for the purposes of Weather Exhaustion.

**Stone Hide.** Your rocky body provides natural protection. Your base Armor Class is **14 + your Constitution modifier**, with no maximum. You cannot wear armor, but you can use shields.

Stone Hide counts as armor for every rule that cares whether you are wearing any: you can gain an armor set's **Set Bonus** while wearing that set's headgear and greaves alone, and you can have Stone Hide itself upgraded at a **Great Fairy Fountain** the way others upgrade a chest piece, to a maximum of ★★ (+2 AC). Features that require you to be unarmored do not work while Stone Hide is active.

**Goron Curl.** As a bonus action, you curl into a rocky sphere and become a rolling weapon. Curling is not a defensive option; it is the wind-up for **Rolling Charge**, and a way to ride out something you cannot dodge.

While curled:
- You have **resistance to bludgeoning, piercing, and slashing damage**, and advantage on Strength and Constitution saving throws.
- You are prone, your speed is 0, you cannot take reactions, and you have disadvantage on Dexterity saving throws.
- The only things you can do are use a bonus action to uncurl, or use a feature that specifically works while curled, such as Rolling Charge.
- Uncurling as a bonus action does not cost movement, and you stand up from prone as part of it without spending movement.

**Rolling Charge.** Starting at 5th level, while curled, you can use your action to roll up to 40 feet. If you move at least 20 feet in a straight line before hitting a creature, it must succeed on a Strength saving throw  
(DC = 8 + your proficiency bonus + your Strength modifier)  
or be knocked prone and take **1d6 bludgeoning damage**.

}}

---

### Goron Subraces

Though all Gorons share a bond with stone and flame, generations of life in different environments have shaped distinct Goron traditions. Most Gorons fall into one of the following subraces.

---

#### Mountain Goron

Mountain Gorons are the most common Gorons found across Death Mountain and similar volcanic ranges. They embody the traditional Goron way of life: miners, guards, and steadfast defenders of their homeland. Where others stumble across loose rock and jagged stone, Mountain Gorons move with practiced confidence.

**Mountain-Born.** You ignore difficult terrain caused by rocky, mountainous, or volcanic environments.

**Immovable Stance.** You have advantage on ability checks and saving throws made to resist being shoved, knocked prone, or forcibly moved.

Mountain Gorons are often chosen as village sentries, caravan guards, and frontline warriors, valued for being reliable and hard to move.

::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::

#### Cave Goron

Cave Gorons dwell deeper beneath the mountains, inhabiting lava tubes, crystal caverns, and ancient mining tunnels. These Gorons tend to have darker stone tones (obsidian, basalt, or iron-rich rock) and are quieter and more contemplative than their surface-dwelling kin.

Accustomed to total darkness and the subtle language of shifting stone, Cave Gorons rely on sound and vibration rather than sight alone.

**Darkvision.** You can see in dim light within 60 feet of you as if it were bright light, and in darkness as if it were dim light.

**Stone Listener.** While you are in contact with stone or earth, you have advantage on Wisdom (Perception) checks that rely on sound or vibration.

Cave Gorons often serve as scouts, tunnel wardens, and guardians of sacred chambers deep within the mountain.

}}

# Hylian

*"Our travels began where most do: at the stables. Beneath towering horse-head effigies and canvas roofs tied with rope, we found the people of Hyrule going about their lives. They listened closely when we spoke, closer than most, and when they prayed it was out of familiarity rather than fear."*

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; — *Viator Fortuitus*  
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; *A Bard's Record, Ch. 01 excerpt*

From rolling plains and forest villages to castle towns and frontier outposts, Hylians are found throughout the lands once touched by the Goddess Hylia. They are explorers, farmers, knights, scholars, and adventurers, shaped by both a divine inheritance and plain mortal stubbornness.

---

### Children of the Goddess

Hylians are descended from the people who once lived alongside the Goddess Hylia herself, before the founding of the Kingdom of Hyrule. This sacred ancestry is most visible in their **long, pointed ears**, said to better hear the voices of the gods.

In ages past, Hylians wielded powerful magic and divine gifts freely. Over centuries, that innate magic faded from most bloodlines. While spellcasters still arise among them, such individuals are rare and often regarded with awe or reverence.

Despite this loss, Hylians retain an unmistakable spiritual sensitivity, a quiet connection to the divine that still shapes their culture and their values.

---

### A People of Many Paths

Hylians vary widely in appearance, temperament, and occupation. They range from barely five feet tall to well over six, with builds as diverse as the lands they inhabit. Their hair and eye colors span nearly every natural shade, though blond hair and light eyes are common in old noble lines.

What unites Hylians is **adaptability**. Where other races are shaped strongly by environment or tradition, Hylians thrive by learning, borrowing, and adapting. They are quick studies and natural generalists.

### Kingdoms, Castles, and Common Folk

Hylian society is highly diverse, ranging from centralized monarchies to scattered rural communities. Castles and cities serve as cultural hubs, but most Hylians live modest lives as farmers, traders, craftsmen, or guards.

Knighthood holds a special place in Hylian culture. Orders sworn to protect the royal family, sacred relics, or the realm itself are common, and many young Hylians grow up dreaming of earning such a title.

Religion remains ever-present. Shrines, temples, and goddess statues dot the land, and prayers to Hylia are simply part of daily life instead of a formal ritual.

---

### The Weight of History

Hylians carry the burden of Hyrule's repeating cycles: kingdoms rising and falling, heroes reborn, evils returning. Most common folk know these stories only as legends, but the truth sits underneath them.

Some Hylians take up adventuring lives out of **duty**, believing it is their role to stand against the darkness when it rises. Others are driven by curiosity, ambition, or the simple desire to see the world beyond their village roads.


### Hylians and Other Races

**Gerudo.** "Fierce, proud, and dangerous to underestimate." Relations range from tense to respectful, shaped by history and politics.

**Gorons.** "Unshakable friends." Hylians value Goron strength and honesty, often relying on them in times of crisis.

**Zora.** "Graceful and distant." Long-standing alliances exist, though cultural differences remain.

**Sheikah.** Trusted protectors and scholars, though their secrecy makes many Hylians uneasy.

**Rito.** Seen as messengers and scouts, free spirits tied more to the sky than the land.

:::::::::::::::::::::

### Hylian Names

Hylian names vary widely by region, culture, and era. Family names are common, particularly among nobles and knights.

**Given Names:** Link, Zelda, Impa, Rauru, Teba, Paya, Mipha, Kass  
**Family Names:** Ardin, Hateno, Ordon, Castleton, Kakariko  
**Titles:** Knight, Captain, Scholar, Warden, Champion

---

### Hylian Traits

Your Hylian character has the following racial traits.

**Creature Type.** You are a Humanoid.

**Ability Score Increase.** You increase one ability score of your choice by 2, and another ability score of your choice by 1.

**Age.** Hylians reach adulthood in their late teens and rarely live beyond 100 years.

**Alignment.** Hylians tend toward no single alignment. Their cultures support a wide range of beliefs, though the ideals of courage, wisdom, and power run all through their history.

**Size.** Hylians vary widely in height and build. Your size is Medium.

**Speed.** Your base walking speed is 30 feet.

**Languages.** You can speak, read, and write Common.

**Versatile Folk.** You gain proficiency in one skill or tool of your choice.

**Great Learners.** You gain one feat of your choice from the following: **Actor, Athlete, Defensive Duelist, Dual Wielder, Dungeon Delver, Durable, Healer, Keen Mind, Lightly Armored, Linguist, Martial Adept, Mobile, Observant, Skilled, Tavern Brawler, Tough.**
