## Other Sacred Relics

### Fused Shadows
*(Twilight Princess)*
*Artifact, Tier 1 (requires attunement) ✦*

Shards of an ancient dark mask holding the magic of the **Dark Interlopers**, the ancestors of the Twili. When the Interlopers tried to seize the Sacred Realm, the Light Spirits sealed their magic into the Fused Shadow at the order of the goddesses. The Fused Shadow is a **prison** rather than a gift, and using it means using what is inside the prison.

*Accounts disagree on whether three or four Light Spirits performed the sealing. They also disagree on how many pieces there are: three were hidden with dungeon guardians, and a fourth was worn openly for years, by an ally, as a helm.*

**Attunement.** Attuning to a shard takes a full day. All shards worn together count as a single attuned item.

**Individual Shards.** While you wear or hold one or more shards, you gain a **+1 bonus to attack and damage rolls**, and advantage on Charisma (Intimidation) checks. **This bonus does not increase with additional shards.**

**Complete Fusion.** With all shards assembled and attuned, once per long rest you can invoke the **True Form** as an action. For 1 minute:

- Your Strength and Constitution become 24 and your size becomes Large.
- You gain 60 temporary hit points.
- You have resistance to all damage.
- You can make two claw attacks with reach 10 feet, each dealing 3d8 + 7 bludgeoning damage.

**Dangerous.** When the True Form ends, make a Wisdom saving throw against your own **Relic save DC**. On a failure you are wrathful and uncontrolled for 1d4 rounds, attacking the nearest creature regardless of allegiance. On your third failure with the same Fused Shadow, the DM decides what you have become.

\column

### Mirror of Twilight
*(Twilight Princess)*
*Artifact, Tier 1 (does not require attunement) ✦*

The link the goddesses left between light and shadow after banishing the Interlopers into the Twilight Realm. It is a **projector, not a portal**: it casts light onto a black Portal Stone, and the stone opens the way.

**Whole Mirror.** Once per day, the restored Mirror opens a two-way gate for 1 minute between its chamber and a corresponding point in the Twilight Realm. Opening it requires either the willing touch of a Twilit creature or a Sage's blessing or equivalent radiant power.

**Individual Shards.** Holding one of the Mirror's shards lets you cast *see invisibility* at will without expending magic points; it reveals Twilit glamours and shadow disguises in particular. You cannot be permanently transformed against your will by Twilight magic.

**A Test of Kingship.** The Mirror can be shattered by force, but only the **true ruler of the Twili** can destroy it utterly. A usurper's strongest magic will only scatter it into shards, and everyone who witnesses that learns exactly what they have witnessed.

---

### Goddess Harp
*(Skyward Sword)*
*Wondrous relic, Tier 3 (requires attunement) ✦*

A small golden harp bearing Hylia's crest, given to the chosen hero by the goddess herself. Playing the right melody on it opens ancient mechanisms and stirs magic that has waited millennia for that exact sequence of notes.

**Effect.** While attuned, you can play the harp as an action to produce one of the following, each once per long rest. Where a saving throw is called for, use your **Relic save DC**.

- **Ballad of the Goddess.** Each sleeping, paralyzed or unconscious ally within 60 feet that can hear the music may immediately repeat one saving throw against an effect causing that condition, ending it on a success. An unconscious ally at 0 hit points instead becomes stable.
- **Farore's Courage.** You and allies within 30 feet who hear the music have advantage on saving throws against being frightened for 1 hour.
- **Nayru's Wisdom.** You gain the benefit of *legend lore* concerning one ancient location or artifact within 1 mile.
- **Din's Power.** Each creature of your choice within 30 feet that can hear the music takes 3d8 thunder damage, or half as much on a successful Constitution saving throw.
- **Awakening.** The harp plays a resonance that activates dormant Sheikah technology, Goddess statues and sealed stone mechanisms. What wakes up is the DM's business.

{{footnote Relics | Other Sacred Relics }}

{{pageNumber,auto}}

\page

## Spiritual Stones
*(Ocarina of Time). Tier 3.*

The three Spiritual Stones are the keys of the Door of Time. Each was held by one of Hyrule's three non-Hylian peoples, and none of them will part with one lightly. *Each requires attunement.*

### Kokiri's Emerald ✦
*Wondrous relic, Tier 3 (requires attunement). Gift of the Great Deku Tree, Stone of the Forest.*

**Passive Effect.** You can speak with and understand plants and beasts. You leave no tracks in forest terrain unless you choose to. Forest-dwelling creatures will not attack you unprovoked.

---

### Goron's Ruby ✦
*Wondrous relic, Tier 3 (requires attunement). Gift of Darunia, Stone of Fire.*

**Passive Effect.** You automatically succeed on Weather Exhaustion checks caused by heat and are immune to fire damage from nonmagical sources. **Once per turn**, when you hit a creature with a melee weapon attack, you deal an additional 1d6 fire damage. You have advantage on Strength (Athletics) checks.

---

### Zora's Sapphire ✦
*Wondrous relic, Tier 3 (requires attunement). Gift of Princess Ruto, Stone of Water.*

**Passive Effect.** You can breathe underwater and have a swim speed of 30 feet. You have advantage on Constitution saving throws. You can speak telepathically with aquatic creatures within 60 feet.

---

**All Three Together.** With the Ocarina of Time and the Song of Time, the three Stones unseal the **Door of Time** in the Temple of Time. In a campaign using the Temple of Time legend, beyond it lies the Pedestal of Time and the Master Sword. In a campaign using the Lost Woods legend, beyond it lies the entrance to the **Sacred Realm** itself, which is a larger and far more dangerous prize.


### Ocarina of Time
*(Ocarina of Time)*
*Artifact, Tier 1 (requires attunement) ✦*

A sky-blue ocarina that belonged to the royal family of Hyrule, holding the echo of every song ever played on it. In the hands of someone who knows the melodies the goddesses wove into Hyrule's fabric, it is among the most powerful objects in the world.

**Attunement.** The ocarina attunes instantly to a bearer it recognizes as of the royal bloodline or chosen by the goddesses. Anyone else must practice for 3 days.

**Songs.** Playing a Song of Power takes an action. Songs must be taught or discovered; the ocarina never reveals one on its own. Where a save is called for, use your **Relic save DC**.

| Song | Effect |
|:--|:--|
| Song of Time | Move Time Blocks (see below). Once per year, rewind to the beginning of the day: everything that happened is undone, and only you remember it |
| Song of Storms | Summon a rainstorm as *control weather*, lasting 1 hour within a mile |
| Saria's Song | Speak telepathically with one named creature, anywhere in the world |
| Epona's Song | Summon a horse bonded to you; it arrives within 10 minutes from wherever it was |
| Minuet of Forest | Teleport to the Sacred Meadow of the Kokiri Forest |
| Bolero of Fire | Teleport to the entrance of Death Mountain's crater |
| Serenade of Water | Teleport to Lake Hylia |
| Nocturne of Shadow | Teleport to the Kakariko Village graveyard |
| Requiem of Spirit | Teleport to the Spirit Temple |
| Prelude of Light | Teleport to the Temple of Time |
| Sonata of Awakening | Each sleeping creature within 30 feet wakes, unless it succeeds on a Constitution saving throw |

> ##### Time Blocks
> **Time Blocks** are pale blue stone blocks marked with the crest of the royal family, found in ruins built by people who expected the Ocarina to still exist when someone came back. They are immovable by any force, magical or physical, and cannot be climbed, destroyed or teleported past.
>
> Playing the **Song of Time** within 30 feet causes every Time Block in range to shift out of phase: a solid block becomes intangible, and an intangible one becomes solid. The change lasts until the song is played again.
>
> They are a lock that only one key opens, and a dungeon full of them is a dungeon that says plainly who it was built for. Use them the way a Zelda dungeon uses them: as a puzzle where the answer is a song, not a strength check.

{{footnote Relics | Stones & Ocarina }}

{{pageNumber,auto}}

\page

## Lesser Relics

Everything before this page changes a campaign. Everything on the next four pages changes a **dungeon**, and that is the more useful thing to have in your hands most weeks.

A Lesser Relic gives a character one new verb: jump, dig, dash, see what is hidden, flip a thing over, walk on water. None of them adds meaningful damage. All of them change what a room can ask of the party, which is the whole engine of a Zelda dungeon and the reason these are worth more at the table than another sword.

**Most Lesser Relics do not require attunement**, so a party can carry many. That is intended. The constraint on a Lesser Relic is not the attunement slot; it is that you have to go and find it.

---

### Lens of Truth ✦
*(Ocarina of Time). Wondrous relic, Tier 4.*

Also called the Eye of Truth. A ring of red-gold holding a violet lens, recovered from the bottom of a well beneath a village where someone with an eye that could see the truth once lived.

**Effect.** As a bonus action you can raise the Lens to your eye. While you look through it, you see invisible creatures and objects, illusions as illusions, false walls, hidden doors, and concealed enemies within 60 feet. You may keep it raised as long as you like, but doing so costs **1 MP or 2 SP at the start of each of your turns**, your choice, and you cannot use the hand holding it.

*The Lens never gates a route. Everything it reveals can also be found by tapping walls and falling into pits. It buys time and skin.*

---

### Book of Mudora
*(A Link to the Past). Wondrous relic, Tier 4.*

A heavy, water-stained collection of ancient Hylian lore, kept for centuries in a village library by people who could not read it.

**Effect.** You can read and understand **ancient Hylian**, the script on monoliths, pedestals, temple walls and sealed doors throughout Hyrule. This is not a translation spell; it is fluency, and it does not run out.

*A great many of Hyrule's relics are locked behind an inscription. The Book is the least impressive item in this chapter and it opens more doors than any three others.*

\column

### Pegasus Boots
*(A Link to the Past). Wondrous relic, Tier 4.*

Heavy bronze-buckled boots that do nothing at a walk and a great deal at a run.

**Effect.** As a bonus action you begin a **dash**: move up to twice your speed in a straight line without provoking opportunity attacks. If you end this movement against a wooden door, a cracked wall, a bookcase, a tree or a similar object, it breaks. If you end it against a creature, it makes a Strength saving throw against your **Relic save DC**, taking 2d6 bludgeoning damage and being pushed 10 feet on a failure, or half damage and no push on a success.

You cannot dash again until the end of your next turn.

---

### Roc's Feather ✦
*(Link's Awakening). Wondrous relic, Tier 4.*

A single stiff white feather, longer than an arm, from a bird nobody living has seen.

**Effect.** Your long jump and high jump distances are doubled, and you may make a running jump after moving only 5 feet rather than 10. As a bonus action you may jump without spending movement.

**With Pegasus Boots.** A creature carrying both may make a **Long Jump**: jump up to your full speed in a straight line as part of a dash, clearing anything between the start and end points.

---

### Power Bracelet
*(The Legend of Zelda). Wondrous relic, Tier 4.*

A plain stone-set bracelet. "This bracelet gives its wearer amazing inner strength. He can even lift giant rocks."

**Effect.** Your carrying capacity, and the weight you can push, drag or lift, are doubled. You can lift and throw objects up to Large size that would otherwise be immovable, including the black stones that seal certain caves. You have advantage on Strength checks made to lift, move or break objects.

---

### Golden Gauntlets ✦
*(Ocarina of Time). Wondrous relic, Tier 3 (requires attunement).*

The Power Bracelet's final ancestor, found in the deepest room of Ganon's own castle. Gold to the elbow and far heavier than they look.

**Effect.** As the Power Bracelet, and in addition your Strength score becomes **21** if it is not already higher. You can lift and hurl objects up to Huge size, including the black monoliths that stand over Hyrule's oldest sealed places.

*At least one of those monoliths has a Great Fairy under it.*

{{footnote Relics | Lesser Relics }}

{{pageNumber,auto}}

\page

### Zora's Flippers
*(A Link to the Past). Wondrous relic, Tier 4.*

Webbed swimming fins of Zora make, traditionally sold rather than given, and never cheaply.

**Effect.** You gain a swim speed equal to your walking speed and can dive to any depth without harm from pressure. You have advantage on Strength (Athletics) checks made to swim, and creatures in the water have disadvantage on attack rolls against you while you are diving.

**With a Zora Ring.** A bearer of both can breathe underwater indefinitely.

---

### Magic Mirror
*(A Link to the Past). Wondrous relic, Tier 4.*

A hand mirror in a curled silver frame, given away by a lost old man to the person who walked him home.

**Effect.** As an action you can activate the Mirror to return from a parallel or overlaid realm (the Twilight Realm, the Dark World, a Silent Realm, the Depths) to the corresponding point in the world of light. Anything you carry and any willing creature you touch comes with you. A shimmering mark remains where you crossed; you can return through it later from either side.

Used inside a dungeon in the ordinary world, the Mirror instead returns you to that dungeon's entrance. It cannot be used to enter a parallel realm, only to leave one.

**Failsafe.** If you are ever trapped in a space you cannot escape, the Mirror activates on its own.

---

### Magic Cape
*(A Link to the Past). Wondrous relic, Tier 3 (requires attunement).*

A dark red cape found under a grave. The person buried there was not the person it was made for.

**Effect.** As a bonus action you may draw the cape around yourself. While it is drawn you are **invisible**, and you may move through creatures, spikes, blades, fire and other hazards without taking damage from them or having your movement stopped.

Drawing the cape costs **2 MP**, and it costs **2 MP more at the start of each of your turns** thereafter. It ends when you stop paying, when you attack, or when you cast a spell.


### Cane of Byrna ✦
*(A Link to the Past). Wondrous relic, Tier 3 (requires attunement).*

A slender blue rod recovered from a cave that could only be reached by jumping off something.

**Effect.** As an action you raise a rotating barrier of light around yourself. While it holds, you have **immunity to all damage**, and any creature that starts its turn within 5 feet of you takes 2d6 force damage.

The barrier costs **3 MP** to raise and **3 MP** at the start of each of your turns to maintain. It ends when you stop paying or when you fall unconscious.

*The Cane costs less than the Magic Cape and hides nothing. Everyone can see exactly where you are, glowing.*

---

### Gust Jar
*(The Minish Cap). Wondrous relic, Tier 4.*

A wide-mouthed clay jar bound in copper, made by people four inches tall, which is why it has a handle on the side rather than the top.

**Effect.** As an action you can direct the jar at a point within 30 feet and either **inhale** or **exhale**.

- **Inhale.** One Small or smaller creature, or one unattended object of up to 25 pounds, is drawn to you unless the creature succeeds on a Strength saving throw against your **Relic save DC**. A creature drawn in is held at the jar's mouth until the start of your next turn, when you may hurl it up to 30 feet as a ranged attack dealing 2d6 bludgeoning damage to it and to whatever it hits.
- **Exhale.** A 15-foot cone of pressurised air. Each creature in it makes the same save or is pushed 10 feet and knocked prone. This extinguishes nonmagical fire and clears loose sand, dust and cobweb from the area.

**Absorption.** As a reaction to being targeted by a fire effect that allows a Dexterity save, you may inhale it instead: you take no damage, and your next Exhale this minute deals 3d6 fire damage in its cone.

---

### Cane of Pacci
*(The Minish Cap). Wondrous relic, Tier 4.*

A short golden cane topped with a crescent, taken from a cave of flames.

**Effect.** As an action, fire a beam at a point within 30 feet. Choose one:

- **Invert an object.** One unattended object of Large size or smaller flips completely over. Pots empty, platforms turn, mine carts right themselves, and certain sealed vessels open only this way.
- **Invert a creature.** One creature of Large size or smaller that is prone, restrained, or has an obvious underside makes a Dexterity saving throw against your **Relic save DC** or is flipped onto its back: prone, and it must use an action to right itself.
- **Charge a hole.** One hole, pit or shaft up to 10 feet across becomes a launcher until the end of your next turn. Any creature entering it is thrown 40 feet straight upward and takes no falling damage from the descent.

{{footnote Relics | Lesser Relics }}

{{pageNumber,auto}}

\page

### Mole Mitts
*(The Minish Cap). Wondrous relic, Tier 4.*

Clawed leather gauntlets found in a fortress in the sky, which is a strange place to keep a digging tool until you learn what they dig through.

**Effect.** You can burrow through packed earth, hard sediment, sand, sealed cave mouths and **cloud barriers** at a rate of 10 feet per minute. The passage stays open behind you. Ten minutes of digging in ordinary ground turns up something: roll on any random treasure table, or hand over a rupee, a beetle, or a shard of something older.

---

### Ball and Chain
*(Twilight Princess). Wondrous relic, Tier 3.*

A spiked iron ball on four feet of chain, taken from a ruined manor in the snow off the body of the thing that was swinging it.

**Effect.** The ball and chain is a martial weapon dealing **2d6 bludgeoning damage** with the **heavy**, **two-handed** and **thrown (range 30/60)** properties. When you throw it, it returns to your hand at the end of your turn, and any creature in the line of its return takes 1d6 bludgeoning damage.

A hit shatters ice, cracks stone and burns away webbing. A Stalfos struck by it is destroyed outright.

**While held.** You have half cover against ranged weapon attacks and cannot be moved by wind or knockback effects. **Your speed is reduced by 10 feet.**

---

### Spinner ✦
*(Twilight Princess). Wondrous relic, Tier 3 (requires attunement).*

An ancient gyroscopic disc from the Arbiter's Grounds, ridden standing, which loses speed the moment you stop feeding it.

**Effect.** As an action you mount the Spinner. For 1 minute:

- Your speed becomes 60 feet, but you must move at least 20 feet in a straight line on each of your turns or the Spinner stops and you dismount.
- You may travel along any **grooved rail**, including vertical and inverted ones, ignoring gravity.
- You cross quicksand, thin ice and collapsing floors without sinking or triggering them.
- As a bonus action you may spin in place: each creature within 5 feet makes a Dexterity saving throw against your **Relic save DC** or takes 2d8 bludgeoning damage and is pushed 10 feet.
- If you mount the Spinner while falling, you descend safely at 60 feet per round and may move 30 feet horizontally per round as you go.

\column

### Dominion Rod ✦
*(Twilight Princess). Wondrous relic, Tier 3 (requires attunement).*

Also called the Rod of the Heavens. The Oocca, the bird-like people who live in the City in the Sky and are said to have shaped Hyrule's first humans, left it with the royal family so that a messenger could speak to the sky. It is unusable until a scholar reads the right passage aloud over it, and it goes quiet again on its own schedule.

**Effect.** As an action, target one statue, automaton or carved figure you can see within 60 feet that is Large size or smaller. Until you take another action to release it, or it is destroyed, it moves as you move and acts on your turn, mirroring you. It has the statistics of an **animated object** of its size, and it can press switches, carry weight, cross hazards and fight.

**The Rod Sleeps.** The Dominion Rod loses its power whenever it leaves the place it was found, and at the DM's discretion at any dramatically appropriate moment. It can only be re-empowered by a scholar reading from the **Ancient Sky Book**, which takes 10 minutes and someone who is not you.

*This is a relic that binds itself to the party's least martial member. That is the point of it.*

---

### The Three Goddess Spells

Three spells the Great Fairies teach, one at each of three fairy fountains, to anyone who reaches them. Each is a **Tier 4 relic** in the form of knowledge rather than an object: once learned it cannot be lost, stolen, or taken by a DM without a very good reason.

**Din's Fire.** *3 MP.* As an action, flame erupts from you in a 15-foot radius. Each creature in it makes a Dexterity saving throw against your **Relic save DC**, taking 4d6 fire damage on a failure or half on a success. Every unlit torch, brazier and lamp in the radius lights at once, which is more often the reason to cast it.

**Nayru's Love.** *6 MP.* As an action, a diamond of blue light surrounds you for 1 minute. You are **immune to all damage** for the duration. You are **not** immune to forced movement, and you cannot cast a spell or use another relic's active effect while it holds.

**Farore's Wind.** *3 MP.* As an action, you set an anchor at your current location, which must be inside a structure you have a map of. As an action thereafter, from anywhere in that structure, you return to the anchor. The anchor lasts until you set another, leave the structure, or become fundamentally other than you were when you set it.

{{footnote Relics | Lesser Relics }}

{{pageNumber,auto}}

\page

### The Three Medallions
*(A Link to the Past). Tier 3.*

Not to be confused with the six **Sage Medallions**, which are gifts, or with any Travel Medallion, which is Sheikah machinery. These three are spells sealed in metal, each waiting under a monolith that has to be read before it will give one up.

Each Medallion is bound to a sword. To use one, you must be holding a sword, and the gesture is part of the spell.

*Each Medallion requires attunement. Where a save is called for, use your Relic save DC.*

### Bombos Medallion ✦
*Wondrous relic, Tier 3 (requires attunement). A monolith in the Desert of Mystery.*

Found by raising a sword to the sky before an inscription only the Book of Mudora can read; the medallion falls from the air.

**Effect.** Once per long rest, as an action, spin your sword in a full circle. A ring of fire races outward, followed by bursting flame. Each creature within 30 feet makes a Dexterity saving throw, taking **6d8 fire damage** on a failure or half on a success. Every flammable object in the radius that is not held or worn catches fire.

---

### Ether Medallion ✦
*Wondrous relic, Tier 3 (requires attunement). A monolith west of the Tower of Hera.*

Raise a sword to the heavens at the inscription and lightning answers, destroying the monolith and leaving the medallion in the crater.

**Effect.** Once per long rest, as an action, raise your sword. The air freezes for a half mile and a storm breaks over a 60-foot radius. Each creature in it makes a Constitution saving throw, taking **6d8 cold damage** on a failure or half on a success. **A flying creature has disadvantage on this save**, and one that fails is also restrained in ice until the end of its next turn.

Ether also clears weather: a storm, fog, or magical precipitation within a mile ends for 1 hour.

\column

### Quake Medallion ✦
*Wondrous relic, Tier 3 (requires attunement). The Lake of Ill Omen.*

Obtained by waking what sleeps in the lake, which is done by throwing a skull into a ring of stones, and which the thing in the lake does not appreciate.

**Effect.** Once per long rest, as an action, drive your sword into the ground. The earth heaves in a 40-foot radius. Each creature on the ground in the area makes a Strength saving throw, taking **6d8 thunder damage** and being knocked prone on a failure, or half damage on a success. Flying creatures are unaffected.

Structures, bridges and unworked stone in the radius take double damage, and the DM may rule that something collapses, opens, or falls in.

---

### Wind Waker ✦
*(The Wind Waker). Artifact, Tier 1 (requires attunement).*

A conductor's baton of white and gold, used long ago to direct the sages who played the song that called upon the gods. It makes no sound of its own; its purpose is to command the people who do.

**Effect.** While attuned, you can conduct as an action. You know the songs below; others exist.

| Song | Effect |
|:--|:--|
| **Wind's Requiem** | Set the prevailing wind's direction within a mile for 1 hour |
| **Song of Passing** | Advance time to the next dawn or dusk, whichever comes first |
| **Ballad of Gales** | Once per long rest, a cyclone carries you and up to eight willing creatures to any location you have previously visited |
| **Command Melody** | As an action, take control of one construct, statue or unattended automaton within 60 feet, or one willing creature. You perceive through it and act as it on your turn while your own body stands still and helpless. Ends as a bonus action, at 1 minute, or if either body takes damage |
| **Earth God's Lyric** | Opens a barrier or seal placed by a Sage of Earth |
| **Wind God's Aria** | Opens a barrier or seal placed by a Sage of Wind |

**Conducting Others.** The Wind Waker's real power is that it does not work alone. When two or more creatures who know a song play it together under your direction, the effect doubles in radius, range or duration, at the DM's discretion. The great works of this baton were all performed by choirs.

# Zelda Dungeon Design Framework

> *"A dungeon is not a monster's home. It is a test. The question is: what is being tested, and who built the exam?"*
> — Field Notes of a Sheikah Scout

Zelda dungeons are unlike standard D&D dungeons. They are not simply dens full of enemies and loot. They are structured experiences, architecturally purposeful spaces that were built for a reason, whether to seal away a sacred power, imprison a great evil, honor a deity, or guard a treasure beyond price. That original purpose shapes everything: the layout, the traps, the enemies, the puzzles, and the final guardian waiting at the heart of it all.

This chapter gives you the tools to build dungeons that feel distinctly Zelda: spaces that reward observation, clever thinking, and mastery of a specific mechanic, while leaving the creative specifics entirely in your hands.

## The Core Philosophy

Before laying out a single room, hold onto three ideas:

**Dungeons have a reason to exist.** Even if the players never learn it, you should know why this place was built. A tomb built to honor a fallen king feels different from a sanctum built to contain a cursed relic, even if both have similar layouts. The reason bleeds into the architecture: a tomb has mourning chambers and offering rooms; a containment sanctum has redundant seals and warning wards. Let the purpose guide your imagination.

**Dungeons teach before they test.** The best Zelda dungeons introduce a mechanic gently, then build on it. The first mirror puzzle is simple. The second adds an enemy. The third combines two mirrors and a moving platform. By the time players reach the boss, they have become fluent in the dungeon's language, and the boss fight is the final exam. Design with this arc in mind.

**Player creativity is not a threat to your dungeon.** It is the point. If a player finds an unexpected solution, your instinct should usually be to let it work. The dungeon's job is to create a feeling (accomplishment, tension, discovery), not to protect a specific sequence of steps. A player who burns down a wooden door has solved a puzzle, just not the one you intended. Embrace it, redirect it, or build gentle consequences into it. But rarely forbid it outright.

{{footnote DM Guide | Dungeon Design }}

{{pageNumber,auto}}

\page

## The Zelda Dungeon Blueprint

The blueprint below is a framework, not a law. Classic Zelda dungeons loop through parts of this sequence multiple times. Some skip steps entirely. Some run the sequence in a different order. Think of it as a checklist of narrative beats, and decide which ones your dungeon needs.

### Step 1: The Entrance

The entrance announces what kind of place this is. It should signal the dungeon's tone immediately, through architecture, atmosphere, ambient sound, or a first encounter that sets the stakes.

A strong entrance typically includes:

- **A landmark or threshold.** Something that marks the boundary between the outside world and the dungeon proper. A massive carved door. A rope bridge over a chasm. A stone archway overgrown with glowing vines. This moment tells players: *we are now inside*.
- **A threshold challenge.** A very small obstacle that does not require the dungeon item to solve. It introduces the dungeon's *atmosphere*, not its mechanic. A simple switch. A vine to climb. A pair of guards. This eases players in without demanding mastery of anything.
- **A first monster encounter.** One to three enemies that establish the dungeon's creature type and fighting style. This is not meant to be dangerous. It is meant to be instructive.

> **Designer's note:** The entrance should feel earned but not draining. Players should feel like they have stepped into something significant, not like they have already spent their resources before the real dungeon begins.

---

### Step 2: Orientation (Map and First Key)

Somewhere in the dungeon's early rooms, players should gain some form of orientation. In classic Zelda, this is the Dungeon Map and Small Key. In your game, this might look like:

- **A schematic inscription** carved into the wall by the dungeon's original builders, not a full map, but enough to hint at the structure.
- **A partial revelation:** a room with windows or interior balconies that lets players see other chambers and begin to understand the layout.
- **A scout opportunity:** a moment where a perceptive or magical player can gather information about what lies ahead (Arcane Eye, a Sheikah Sensor ping, a successful Perception check from a high vantage point).
- **A first locked door** or equivalent gated passage that signals there is a key to find.

Players do not need a complete map. They need enough information to feel like they are exploring rather than wandering.

---

### Step 3: The Mini-Boss

Roughly one-third to halfway through the dungeon, players encounter a significant combat challenge, not the final boss, but something that demands more than a standard encounter. The mini-boss serves two purposes:

**First**, it is a skill check on how players have adapted to the dungeon environment so far.

**Second**, it guards the dungeon's signature item.

The mini-boss should feel thematically tied to the dungeon. It does not have to be a unique creature. A heavily armored Darknut in a warrior's tomb, a massive Deku Baba at the heart of a corrupted grove, an elite Silver Moblin commanding a fortified chamber: any of these works, as long as it feels like it belongs in this dungeon and not on a random encounter table.

> **Reward:** When the mini-boss falls, players find, or gain access to, the Dungeon Item.

---

### Step 4: The Dungeon Item

The Dungeon Item is the heart of a Zelda dungeon. It is the tool that unlocks the second half of the dungeon, solves its central puzzles, and determines the strategy for the boss fight.

**Choosing a Dungeon Item:** Pick something from the Adventuring Gear chapter that creates interesting *interactions with the environment*, not just combat power. Good Dungeon Items have answers to the question: *"What can I do with this that I couldn't do before?"*

Examples:
- **Hookshot:** Pull objects, cross gaps, reach high switches, yank enemies.
- **Boomerang:** Hit multiple targets or distant switches, stun enemies briefly, retrieve items.
- **Bombs:** Destroy cracked walls, stun enemies, solve weight puzzles, trigger timed sequences.
- **Bow:** Hit distant eye-switches, pop air-based targets, fire elemental arrows at themed obstacles.
- **Lens of Truth:** Reveal hidden passages, see through illusions, identify concealed enemies.

**Introducing the Item:** The room where players find the dungeon item should immediately suggest one obvious use for it. A Hookshot found in a room with a large metal ring on a distant platform. Bombs found next to a visibly cracked wall. Do not let players wonder what it does; show them.

{{footnote DM Guide | Dungeon Design }}

{{pageNumber,auto}}

\page

**Teaching the Item:** Rooms between the mini-boss and the boss should progressively deepen how the item is used:

| Room | What It Teaches |
|:--|:--|
| First puzzle room | The item's simplest function (pull/throw/light) |
| Second puzzle room | Combining the item with an enemy encounter |
| Third puzzle room | Using the item in a time-pressured or sequential way |
| Final pre-boss room | A complex application that foreshadows the boss strategy |

Players should arrive at the boss door feeling *fluent* in the item, not still figuring it out.

---

### Step 5: Escalation and Exploration

The bulk of the dungeon lies between the Dungeon Item and the Boss Key. This is where the dungeon breathes. Use this space for:

- **Backtracking with new eyes.** Doors or passages the players noticed early but couldn't open are now accessible with the dungeon item. This rewards exploration and creates satisfying "aha" moments.
- **Hidden caches.** Optional rooms containing rupees, potions, spare keys, or lore. These are for players who explore thoroughly. Never block the critical path behind optional content.
- **Environmental hazards.** Pressure plates, falling ceilings, spike corridors, darkness, fire jets. These should feel like part of the dungeon's original purpose, not arbitrary obstacles.
- **Secondary enemies.** Introduce variants or companion creatures to the ones seen at the entrance. A dungeon that started with Keese now adds Fire Keese in the deeper chambers.

> **The Boss Key equivalent** is found somewhere in this section: a distinct item, rune, ward, or combination of keys that unlocks the final chamber. Its placement is a reward for thorough exploration of the dungeon's second half.

---

### Step 6: The Boss Chamber

The boss chamber should feel architecturally different from the rest of the dungeon. Larger. More deliberate. A space that was designed to contain something.

**Before the door:** A moment of transition: a save point, a chest with a potion or two, a healing pool, a moment of eerie quiet. This is a grace beat. It signals that what comes next is significant.

**The boss fight:** See the *Zelda Boss Design* chapter for full guidance on structuring boss phases, communicating weaknesses, and running vulnerability windows. For dungeon design purposes, ensure:

- The boss fight takes place in an environment that allows creative use of the dungeon item.
- The boss's weakness is connected to that same item, completing the dungeon's thematic arc.
- The chamber has enough space and features for dynamic movement (platforms, hazards, destructible elements) to prevent the fight from becoming a static damage race.

---

### Step 7: The Reward

After the boss falls, the dungeon resolves. The reward is both narrative and mechanical.

**Mechanical rewards** may include:
- A **Heart Container equivalent:** a permanent +2 maximum HP bonus, one additional Hit Die, or a permanent Stamina Point.
- A **relic, medallion, pendant, or sacred artifact** tied to the campaign's main quest.
- A significant **rupee cache**, rare materials, or unique equipment.
- A **new capability:** access to a region, a fast-travel shrine, or an NPC alliance unlocked by the dungeon's completion.

**Narrative rewards** matter equally: the dungeon's purpose is resolved. The seal holds. The corruption is cleansed. The treasure is claimed. Give this a moment. Let it land.

{{footnote DM Guide | Dungeon Design }}

{{pageNumber,auto}}

\page

## Central Mechanics (Optional)

Some dungeons are built around a single environmental mechanic that transforms how every room is navigated. This is not required. Many excellent dungeons have no central mechanic beyond the dungeon item itself, but when used well, a central mechanic can make a dungeon feel completely unlike anything else in the campaign.

If you choose to use one, introduce it before the mini-boss so players have time to understand it before they need to use it under pressure.

| Mechanic | How It Works in Play |
|:--|:--|
| **Water Levels** | A central switch or sequence of valves raises or lowers water throughout the dungeon, opening new passages and closing others. Some rooms are only accessible when flooded; others only when drained. |
| **Wind Currents** | Fans, vents, or pressure plates create or redirect air currents that players can ride (with the right item) or must navigate around. Enemies may be carried by currents too. |
| **Mirrors and Light** | A light source exists in one room. Mirrors or prisms must be rotated or positioned to direct beams to activate switches, open doors, or illuminate hidden passages. |
| **Gravity Shifts** | Certain rooms or floors have reversed or altered gravity. Players walk on ceilings, enemies fall upward, and puzzle solutions require thinking about orientation in three dimensions. |
| **Time or State Changes** | The dungeon exists in two states — past and present, day and night, cursed and uncursed — and players switch between them via a mechanic. What is a locked door in one state may be a rubble pile in the other. |
| **Elemental Transformation** | The dungeon responds to elemental manipulation. Ice melts to water which fills channels which powers mechanisms. Fire spreads along oil trails. Lightning conducted through metal rods activates circuits. |
| **Invisible Architecture** | Walls, bridges, or platforms are invisible or revealed only through a specific item (Lens of Truth), ability, or action. Navigation requires memory and careful movement. |

> **Rule of escalation:** Whatever your central mechanic is, introduce it in its simplest form within the first three rooms. Every subsequent encounter with it should add one layer of complexity.

\column

## Puzzle Design Philosophy

Puzzles are the creative language of a Zelda dungeon. Before worrying about specific puzzle designs, internalize these principles. They will guide every puzzle you build.

### The Rule of Player Agency

The puzzle exists to create a moment of discovery, not to protect a specific solution. When you design a puzzle, ask yourself: *"What is the feeling I want players to have when they solve this?"* Then build backwards from that feeling. If a player achieves that feeling through an unexpected method, they have solved the puzzle.

**Players will break your puzzles.** They will burn doors, knock over pillars, cast spells you didn't consider, use racial abilities in unexpected ways, and generally apply creative lateral thinking to every problem you place in front of them. This is not a problem. It is the game working correctly.

You should almost always allow creative solutions. The question is *what the world's response is* when they do.

{{footnote DM Guide | Dungeon Design }}

{{pageNumber,auto}}

\page

### Responding to Player Creativity: The DM's Options

When a player solves a puzzle in an unexpected way, you have several tools available. None of these is universally correct. Choose based on what serves the moment and your table's preferences.

| Situation | Option A: Embrace It | Option B: Consequence | Option C: Redirect |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Players burn down a wooden puzzle door | The door opens. They proceed. Reward creative thinking. | The fire spreads to adjacent room, alerting enemies or triggering a trap. | The door is fireproofed (magical lacquer), or fire damage causes it to seal tighter. |
| Players bypass a switch puzzle by moving the target object directly | It works. They're clever. Move on. | The object is heavier than expected — Strength check required. On failure, they need the intended method. | The object is warded — it cannot be moved without the switch being activated first. |
| Players try to dig under a sealed door | It works, into a 1-foot crawlspace. They squeeze through. | The floor is stone — they need an Earth Sage or specific tool. | Below the door is a pressure plate that activates something else when stepped on. |
| Players use a spell the dungeon wasn't designed for | It works, and you improvise a reasonable outcome. | The dungeon's wards create magical interference — spell save DC increased inside. | The spell produces an unexpected side effect tied to the dungeon's theme. |

> **The golden rule:** A creative solution that bypasses a puzzle entirely is almost always better to allow than to deny. Players who feel clever are players who are having fun. Players who feel railroaded are players who disengage.

### The Hint System: INT and WIS Rolls

When players are genuinely stuck, not just impatient, but truly at an impasse, the hint system gives you a structured way to help without removing the challenge.

**When to offer it:** Wait for a natural pause. If players have been discussing a puzzle for several minutes without progress and the energy at the table is starting to flag, that is the moment.

**How to frame it:** *"You've been studying this chamber for a while. Anyone want to make an Intelligence or Wisdom check to see if you notice something you might have missed?"* (DC 12–15 depending on difficulty of the puzzle.)

**On a success:** Offer a hint that narrows the solution space without solving it outright. *"You notice that the shadow the statue casts doesn't quite match the light source in the room."* The players still have to figure out what to do with that information.

**On a failure:** You have two options, and both are valid:
- **No information:** *"You study the room carefully but don't find anything new."* This maintains tension but may frustrate players further, so use it sparingly.
- **Misdirection:** *"Your eye is drawn to the large crystal on the far wall, but something about the floor near the entrance feels slightly off too."* This gives players something to chase that may or may not be relevant, keeping engagement high without solving anything.

> **Never offer the full solution.** A hint that eliminates all remaining uncertainty is not a hint. It's you solving the puzzle for them. The goal is to restart the engine of creative thinking, not to replace it.

### Designing Puzzle-Proof Dungeons

Some puzzle vulnerabilities are worth thinking through before your session. A few questions to ask yourself for each puzzle:

- **What is the obvious solution?** Make sure it works cleanly.
- **What is the unintended brute-force solution?** Decide in advance whether it works, costs something, or has a consequence.
- **Can a specific class feature, spell, or racial ability trivialize this?** If a Rito can simply fly over a gap puzzle, is that okay? (Usually: yes.) Does the puzzle have a version that still engages the Rito player even though flight solves the traversal? Consider that.
- **What happens if players do nothing?** Some puzzles should have a consequence for inaction (the floor descends, a timer triggers). Others are fine left unsolved indefinitely.
- **Is there a secondary solution for players without the dungeon item?** This rarely comes up, but if players somehow bypass the mini-boss and haven't found the item yet, make sure the dungeon doesn't hard-lock.

{{footnote DM Guide | Dungeon Design }}

{{pageNumber,auto}}

\page

## Quick-Build Checklist

Use this when designing any dungeon from scratch.

**Before you build:**
- [ ] What was this dungeon originally built for?
- [ ] What is its external environment and how does that affect its interior?
- [ ] Does it have a Central Mechanic? If so, what is it?
- [ ] What is the Dungeon Item?
- [ ] What is the boss, and how does the Dungeon Item defeat it?

**Rooms to include (minimum viable dungeon, 7 rooms):**
- [ ] Entrance chamber (threshold + first encounter)
- [ ] Orientation room (map/structure hint + first locked passage)
- [ ] Mini-boss chamber (guards the Dungeon Item)
- [ ] Dungeon Item room (item found + immediate use demonstrated)
- [ ] Puzzle room 1 (simple use of item)
- [ ] Puzzle room 2 (combined use: item + enemy or item + environment)
- [ ] Boss chamber (item-based weakness, dynamic space)

**For each puzzle, confirm:**
- [ ] At least two valid solutions exist
- [ ] Brute-force approach has a planned response
- [ ] Class-specific abilities won't hard-break it (or you've decided that's fine)
- [ ] A hint path exists if players get stuck

**For the boss fight, confirm:**
- [ ] The weakness is tied to the Dungeon Item
- [ ] The arena has enough space and features for dynamic combat
- [ ] There is a vulnerability window that rewards observant play
- [ ] The reward is meaningful and feels like the dungeon's completion

{{footnote DM Guide | Dungeon Design }}

{{pageNumber,auto}}

\page

## Example Dungeon: The Thornheart Sanctum

*A complete worked example using the framework above.*

**Background:** Deep in the Faron Rainforest, an ancient grove was sealed by the Deku elders three centuries ago when a Great Deku Baba, an enormous, semi-intelligent carnivorous plant, took root in the sanctum's heart and began corrupting the surrounding forest. The sanctum was built originally as a meditation retreat for forest-attuned Sages. Its architecture reflects that origin: open vine-lattice walls, root-threaded floors, chambers full of natural light. Now, corrupted plant-growth has twisted it into something predatory.

**Recommended party level:** 2–4
**Recommended party size:** 3–5
**Dungeon Item:** Boomerang (found on the body of a petrified Deku sage in the mini-boss room)
**Central Mechanic:** None (straightforward, ideal teaching dungeon)
**Estimated sessions:** 1–2

---

### Room 1: The Strangled Gate (Entrance)

*The sanctum's entrance is an arched doorway of living wood, now choked with thick, pulsing vines. Two Deku Babas flank the path, their stems embedded in the soil on either side.*

**First encounter:** 2× Deku Baba (CR 1/4 each). These introduce the Deku Baba's Weak Point: Called Shot (Stem). Players who target the stem prevent the Baba from using its Snap attack. This is a gentle tutorial for the called shot system in an appropriately low-stakes encounter.

**Threshold puzzle:** The gate itself is sealed by a vine-wrapped locking mechanism, a thick woven knot of corrupted plant matter. Options:
- **Intended:** Cutting the vines with a slashing weapon (2 rounds of sustained cutting or one Called Shot).
- **Creative:** Burning the vines (fire damage ignites them, but also risks alerting deeper residents; DM's call on whether this draws a patrol).
- **Clever:** A Deku PC can use Deku Spit to break apart the dry outer vines before cutting, reducing it to 1 round.

*The gate groans open. The air inside smells of rot and wet soil.*

\column

### Room 2: The Meditation Hall (Orientation)

*A wide, high-ceilinged chamber. Stone plinths hold carved bowls that once contained water, now dry and cracked. On the far wall, a schematic of the sanctum is carved in relief: six chambers arranged around a central root-cluster, with a larger space at the heart. One door to the north is sealed with a runed wooden bar. One door to the west is open.*

**Orientation:** The carved schematic gives players a rough map: six rooms, one locked northern passage, one open western path, and something significant at the center. They don't need to understand everything. They just need to know there's a structure.

**Locked door (north):** The runed wooden bar is magically reinforced. It cannot be broken, burned, or bypassed by normal means. It reacts to the sound of something specific (revealed later to be the boomerang's returning spin, which the Deku elders used as a key tone). Players may note it but cannot open it yet.

**Encounter:** 3× Deku Scrub in hiding (Shrub Disguise; they appear as plants). One Perception check (DC 13) reveals the ambush before it triggers. If missed, they attack when players examine the locked door. The Deku Scrubs attempt to flee underground when reduced to half HP, if captured or spoken to (Speak with Animals or Deku PC), they can confirm: *"The winding thing opens the sealed ways. The round-thrower. The spinning sage-tool."* This is a hint toward the Dungeon Item without revealing it.

---

### Room 3: The Root Corridor

*A narrow passage choked with root growth. The roots form a deliberate maze. This was clearly architectural at one point. Now the corruption has thickened them into near-solid walls of writhing plant matter. Some sections of the root-wall pulse faintly with dark energy.*

**Environmental hazard:** Moving through the root corridor costs 1 extra foot of movement per foot traveled (difficult terrain). A creature can spend 1 Stamina Point to ignore this for 5 feet.

**Puzzle:** Three sections of the corridor are blocked by particularly dense root-clusters. Each cluster has a visible dry, brown core, the corrupted heartwood. Hitting the core with piercing or slashing damage kills the cluster (AC 12, 10 HP). The puzzle is recognizing that the cores need to be targeted specifically and that the surrounding root mass has resistance to bludgeoning damage (it compresses rather than breaks).

**Alternative:** A Sage with Plant Growth or Speak with Plants can address the corruption directly. On a successful DC 13 Wisdom check they can calm one cluster enough to pass without combat.

{{footnote DM Guide | Dungeon Design }}

{{pageNumber,auto}}

\page

### Room 4: The Petrified Archive (Mini-Boss)

*A circular chamber. Shelves of root-bound scrolls line the walls, most rotted beyond reading. At the center, a Deku elder has been entirely petrified by the Great Baba's corruption, wooden and still, one arm extended as if offering something. In its frozen hand: a carved boomerang, still gleaming.*

**Mini-boss:** Corrupted Armos (use the Armos stat block, refluffed as a Guardian Statue carved from living wood, a protective construct the Deku elders awakened). Its Weak Point is its Core Rune, visible on its chest.

*The statue's eyes glow amber. It moves.*

The fight teaches players to notice and target the Core Rune weak point. When the Core Rune takes a Called Shot hit, the statue is stunned until the start of its next turn, creating the vulnerability window. When defeated, the amber light goes out. The statue is still.

**Reward:** The Boomerang in the petrified elder's hand is now accessible. When a player takes it, a soft chime resonates through the room, and in the distance, through the walls, they hear a brief resonant hum from the direction of the sealed northern door.

> **DM note:** The chime is a deliberate auditory hint, the boomerang's tone is connected to the rune-locked door. Players may not understand it yet, but they should note it.

---

### Room 5: The Still Pool (Puzzle Room 1: Simple)

*A chamber bisected by a 10-foot gap. On the far side, a stone lever sits beside a sealed gate. Between here and there: open air over a deep root-filled pit.*

**Intended solution:** Throw the boomerang at the lever on the far side to pull/activate it. The boomerang's return arc is the key. It hooks the lever on the throw and pulls it on the return.

**Alternative solutions:**
- A Hookshot (if somehow acquired) can reach the lever.
- A ranged spell attack that hits the lever (DM adjudicates whether the lever responds to impact; yes, at disadvantage, since it's designed for the boomerang's hook).
- A Rito PC can fly across.
- The Boomerang still works better: if players use it, the gate opens smoothly. Alternative solutions may open the gate partway, requiring a second attempt.

**Puzzle-break protection:** The gap is too wide to jump without the Jump spell. The walls beside the gap are slick with moisture (Acrobatics DC 16 to traverse them), and a failed Dexterity save means 1d6 fall damage and landing in the root-pit (difficult terrain, requires a Strength DC 12 Athletics check to climb out).

---

### Room 6: The Spore Garden (Puzzle Room 2: Combined)

*A greenhouse chamber. Corrupted spores fill the air. Each creature that ends its turn here makes a DC 10 Constitution save or takes 1d4 poison damage. Three large seed-pods hang from vines at the ceiling, swollen and dark. A locked gate on the far wall has three small indentations above it, clearly designed to receive something.*

**Encounter:** 2× Green Bokoblin patrol, using the spore cloud as cover (they're immune; they belong here). Players dealing with both the Bokoblins and the environmental hazard simultaneously.

**Puzzle:** The three seed-pods, when struck with the boomerang, release a hardened seed that flies toward the corresponding indentation in the gate, locking into place. All three must be hit in sequence (the gate resets if more than 10 seconds, 2 rounds, pass between activations).

**Teaching moment:** This is the first time players must use the boomerang in a sequence under time pressure and while managing combat. The Bokoblins are not so threatening that the puzzle becomes impossible, but they create enough pressure to make it interesting.

**Alternative:** Players who clear the Bokoblins first, then solve the puzzle without time pressure, also succeed. The sequence mechanic is forgiving enough to allow this.

**Spore hazard interaction:** A character can spend an action to cover their face with cloth, gaining advantage on the Constitution saves. A Water-type spell or Create or Destroy Water cast at the ceiling clears the spores from a 10-foot section of the room.

---

### Room 7: The Sealed Way (Back to Room 2: Backtrack)

*Returning through the Meditation Hall, players now hold the boomerang. The runed wooden bar on the northern door pulses faintly when the boomerang is brought near.*

**Callback puzzle:** Players must throw the boomerang at the runed bar. On the return arc, the boomerang passes through the rune's field, vibrating at the correct resonant frequency. The bar dissolves. The northern passage opens.

This is a deliberate backtrack. Players re-enter a space they've seen before and solve something they couldn't before. The "click" of retroactive understanding is a core Zelda satisfaction: *we needed this all along.*

{{footnote DM Guide | Dungeon Design }}

{{pageNumber,auto}}

\page

### Boss Chamber: The Thornheart

*A massive domed chamber. The ceiling is open to the sky, or what was once sky, now a canopy of corrupted root-growth that blocks all light except for a single shaft at the center. In that shaft of filtered green light, the Great Deku Baba coils.*

*It is enormous. Its stem is as thick as a tree trunk, its maw wide enough to swallow a horse. Amber-corrupt light pulses through the veins running up its body. Its eyes, four of them, open slowly.*

**Boss:** The Thornheart (Great Deku Baba; use a modified Deku Baba stat block at CR 5–6, or build a custom boss using the Boss Design chapter as a guide).

**Weak Point:** The amber-glowing **Bulb Node** at the base of its stem, the crystallized corrupted core from which all its power radiates.

**Phase 1: Flailing.** The Thornheart attacks with its Snap bite and sweeping Stem Lash. Its Bulb Node is buried in root-growth and not yet visible. Players must deal 20 damage to force the first vulnerability window.

**Vulnerability Window 1:** The Thornheart rears back in pain, its Bulb Node briefly exposed and glowing. Players have until the start of the Thornheart's next turn to target it. A Called Shot (Bulb Node) stuns the Thornheart until the end of its turn and deals double damage dice.

**Phase 2: Rooted Defense.** At half HP, the Thornheart drives its stem into the floor, becoming Rooted (cannot be moved, but gains +3 AC from its bark tightening). It begins launching Seed Volleys, ranged attacks that deal 1d8 piercing damage to creatures in a 10-foot line. Its Bulb Node is now only exposed during Seed Volley recharge (every other round).

**Using the Boomerang:** The Thornheart's Bulb Node can only be reliably exposed by hitting one of its four Eyes with the boomerang, causing the Thornheart to reflexively recoil and expose the Node for one round. Players who figure this out gain a reliable way to create vulnerability windows on demand. Players who don't figure it out must wait for the natural recharge windows.

> **DM note:** If players are struggling with Phase 2, a DC 13 Wisdom check as a hint roll reveals: *"The creature's eyes seem to respond to the boomerang. Each impact makes it flinch. Maybe forcing a reaction could expose its core."*

**Defeat:** When the Thornheart reaches 0 HP, the amber corruption drains from its body. The great plant collapses, its roots withdrawing into the floor. The canopy cracks open, real sunlight pouring down. The room begins to smell of clean rain and green growth.

The corruption is broken.

\column

### Reward

**Mechanical:**
- **Heart of the Grove:** Each player gains +2 to their maximum hit points (permanent). This represents the sanctum's blessing, the grove recognizing its liberators.
- **Thornheart Seed:** A rare crafting component. A Deku PC or Sage of Earth affinity can identify its properties with a DC 13 Nature check. It can be used to craft a Seed of Renewal (single-use: restore a dying plant to full health, or purify a small area of Malice corruption).
- **Rupee Cache:** 180 rupees in ancient Deku amber-coins (accepted at most merchants), plus 2 Deku Sticks and a vial of Deku Oil.

**Narrative:**
The petrified elder in Room 4, the one from whose hand the boomerang was taken, slowly, over the next hour, begins to soften. They will not fully recover for several days, but as players leave, they see the wood of the elder's fingers uncurl. Life is returning.

Whatever quest brought them to this forest, the sanctum now rests.

{{footnote DM Guide | Dungeon Design }}

{{pageNumber,auto}}

\page

# Zelda Boss Design

> *"The dungeon is a sentence. The boss is the period. Everything before it was building toward this moment, and the players know it."*
> — Field Notes of a Sheikah Scout

A Zelda boss fight is not a standard D&D encounter with a big HP pool. It is a structured performance, a puzzle wrapped in combat, with a rhythm of tension, revelation, and payoff that repeats until the creature falls. When designed well, a boss fight feels like the dungeon's final argument: everything the players learned inside this place was preparation for exactly this moment.

This chapter gives you the tools to design boss fights that feel distinctly Zelda, built on discovery, exploitation, vulnerability, and the damage window, and scaling from a simple two-phase encounter at low levels to a full three-phase spectacle at the campaign's climax.

---

## The Boss Loop

Every Zelda boss fight is built around a repeating loop of four beats. Each phase of the fight runs through this loop once before the boss transitions. Understanding the loop is the foundation of everything else.

```
DISCOVERY → EXPLOITATION → VULNERABILITY → DAMAGE WINDOW
     ↑                                              |
     └──────────────── (repeat per phase) ──────────┘
```

{{footnote DM Guide | Boss Design }}

{{pageNumber,auto}}

\page

### Beat 1: Discovery

Players must understand *how this fight works* before they can win it. Discovery is the moment, or series of moments, where that understanding clicks into place.

Discovery can be:

**Self-evident.** Some weak points require no explanation. A massive glowing eye begs to be shot. A monster encased in ice clearly hates fire. A skeleton animated by a glowing gem will fall when the gem is destroyed. Players familiar with the Zelda series will often spot these immediately, and that recognition is its own reward. Let it land without over-explaining.

**Environmental.** The arena itself hints at the solution. Oil channels on the floor suggest fire. A pool of water suggests lightning will conduct. A ceiling full of stalactites suggests something heavy dropping. The dungeon item the players just found is almost always relevant, if they have a boomerang, something in this room can be hit with a boomerang.

**Behavioral.** The boss reveals its weakness through its own actions. It opens its mouth to roar, exposing the soft interior. It charges and buries its horns in the wall, leaving itself momentarily stuck. It rises to full height for a devastating leap, exposing the underside. Good behavioral tells communicate *and* feel like organic creature behavior simultaneously.

**Emergent.** Players discover the weakness through experimentation. They try things. Something works. This is the least reliable form of discovery and should be used carefully. Players who feel like they're guessing without feedback will disengage. If you rely on emergent discovery, build in partial responses to incorrect attempts: *the creature flinches when struck with fire* is feedback even if fire isn't the final answer.

> **The DM's job during Discovery:** Watch the table. If players are clearly engaged and theorizing, stay quiet and let them work. If energy is flagging and the fight is starting to feel like an attrition grind, trigger the hint system (see below).

**Hint Rolls During Discovery:**

When players are genuinely stuck, not just impatient, but truly unable to identify how the fight is supposed to work, offer the hint roll.

*"You've been fighting this creature for several rounds without finding an opening. Anyone want to make an Intelligence or Wisdom check to see if something about it stands out?"* (DC 12–15 depending on boss complexity.)

| Result | DM Response |
|:--|:--|
| Success | A specific, actionable observation that narrows the solution without solving it outright. *"The creature's hide seems to harden whenever it stands still — but when it charges, you notice the joints at its shoulders loosen considerably."* |
| Failure (no information) | *"You study its movements carefully but can't find a pattern yet."* Use sparingly — this maintains tension but risks frustrating players further. |
| Failure (misdirection) | Give players something to investigate that may be partially useful or adjacent to the real answer. *"Your eye is drawn to the glowing marks on the floor — they seem to pulse when the creature moves across them."* Keeps engagement high without solving anything. |

---

### Beat 2: Exploitation

Once players understand the weak point, they must *do something* to expose it. Exploitation is the active, mechanical step between knowledge and reward.

Exploitation should require effort: enough that landing it feels like an accomplishment, but not so much that it becomes frustrating.

Common exploitation patterns:

| Exploitation Type | What Players Do | Example |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Projectile to weak point** | Aim and fire at a specific target during a window | Shooting an eye with a bow while it stares at you |
| **Item interaction** | Use the dungeon item in a specific way | Hooking a boss's tail with the hookshot to stop its spin |
| **Environmental trigger** | Use the arena to create the opening | Luring the boss onto a pressure plate that stuns it |
| **Behavioral bait** | Provoke the boss into a self-exposing action | Standing near a wall to bait a charge that lodges its horns |
| **Elemental response** | Apply the correct element to reveal or expose | Melting ice armor with fire spells to reveal the core beneath |
| **Team coordination** | Multiple players acting in concert | One player distracts, another flanks to hit the exposed rear |

> **Design principle:** Exploitation should feel active, not passive. Players should be *doing* something, not waiting for the boss to expose itself on a timer. The best exploitations require the players to make a decision and take a risk.

{{footnote DM Guide | Boss Design }}

{{pageNumber,auto}}

\page

### Beat 3: Vulnerability

Successful exploitation creates a **Vulnerability Window**, a brief period where the boss is exposed, staggered, stunned, or otherwise open to significant damage.

The Vulnerability Window is the emotional peak of each loop. It is the moment players have been working toward, and it should *feel* significant:

- **Narrate the shift.** *"The Thornheart's stem buckles, the amber node at its base pulses open, glowing bright. The corruption flickers."* Give players a clear visual signal that the window is open.
- **Make it time-limited.** The window should last long enough for players to act meaningfully, typically until the end of the boss's next turn, or until a specific trigger closes it. Not so long that it loses urgency; not so short that it becomes a reflex test.
- **Scale it to the phase.** Early vulnerability windows in Phase 1 might be generous. By Phase 3, windows may be shorter or require more precise positioning.

**Called Shots during Vulnerability:** A Called Shot against the exposed weak point during a Vulnerability Window should deal additional dice and apply the full Critical Hit effect from the monster's stat block. This is the design intent of the system, called shots during vulnerability windows are the primary damage mechanism of a Zelda boss fight.

---

### Beat 4: The Damage Window

The Damage Window is when everyone unloads. This is not the vulnerability window itself. It is the immediate aftermath, when the boss is staggered and players have already landed their big hit. For 1–2 rounds after a successful exploitation, the boss may have reduced AC, be prone, lose its reaction, or otherwise be easier to damage than normal.

The Damage Window closes when:
- The boss recovers and resets (standing up, resealing its weak point, resuming its patrol pattern)
- A phase transition triggers
- The boss is defeated

> **Pacing note:** The loop should feel rhythmic. Discovery is slow and tense. Exploitation is active and exciting. Vulnerability is a burst of adrenaline. The Damage Window is satisfying follow-through. Then the boss resets, and the loop begins again, with slight variations to keep it from becoming rote.

\column

## Phase Design

Most Zelda bosses have **two to three phases**. Stronger, more narratively significant bosses may have more. A simple dungeon guardian might have only one phase with a straightforward vulnerability loop.

### Phase Count by Boss Tier

| Boss Tier | Phases | When to Use |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Dungeon Guardian** (CR 3–5) | 1–2 | Minor dungeons, early campaign, first-time players |
| **Temple Boss** (CR 6–9) | 2–3 | Standard dungeon finale, mid-campaign |
| **Calamity Lieutenant** (CR 10–14) | 3 | Named villains, major story beats |
| **Final Boss / Ganon-tier** (CR 15+) | 3–4+ | Campaign climax, once-per-campaign |

### Phase Transitions

A boss transitions to its next phase when it crosses an HP threshold. The standard thresholds are:

| Phase Count | Transition Points |
|:--|:--|
| 2 phases | 50% HP |
| 3 phases | 66% and 33% HP |
| 4 phases | 75%, 50%, and 25% HP |

**Phase skipping:** If players deal enough burst damage to drop the boss past a threshold in a single round (from 70% to 25% in one turn, for example), you have two options:

- **Skip the phase:** The boss jumps straight to its final phase, bypassing the middle one entirely. Reward decisive play. The fight ends faster.
- **Compress the phase:** The transition triggers immediately, but the skipped phase's mechanics are folded briefly into the current one: the boss uses one ability from each simultaneously before settling into its final form.

Both are valid. Decide based on which makes the moment feel more dramatic.

{{footnote DM Guide | Boss Design }}

{{pageNumber,auto}}

\page

### Types of Phase Transitions

Phase transitions are one of the most important moments in a boss fight. They should feel significant, a clear signal that the fight has changed, and that what worked before may not work the same way now.

**Cosmetic + Tactical (same arena, new behavior)**
The most common transition. The boss's appearance changes and it gains new attacks or loses old ones. The arena stays the same; the players' strategy must adapt.

*Examples:*
- A Darknut loses its outer armor layer, revealing a faster, more aggressive fighter beneath.
- A corrupted plant boss sheds its bark shell and begins fighting as a writhing core of roots.
- An undead knight's sword ignites, adding fire damage to its strikes.

Best for: Earlier phase transitions, lower-CR bosses, or when you want to preserve momentum.

**Environmental**
The arena itself changes at the transition: new hazards appear, existing features are altered, or the physical space shifts. This forces players to adapt to both the new boss behavior and the new environment simultaneously.

*Examples:*
- Water floods the chamber floor (difficult terrain, creatures can drown if knocked prone).
- Platforms collapse, reducing the traversable area.
- A second wind source activates, redirecting air-based mechanics.
- The lighting changes: the room goes dark except for the boss's bioluminescence.

Best for: Mid-campaign bosses, dungeons with central mechanics, or when you want the transition to feel catastrophic.

**Full Transformation (rare)**
The boss becomes something fundamentally different: a different form, a different creature, or an entirely new threat. This is reserved for the most climactic encounters in the campaign.

*Examples:*
- Ganondorf, defeated in humanoid form, rises as Ganon, a massive boar-demon with entirely different attacks, weak points, and required strategies.
- A possessed temple guardian shatters, releasing the dark spirit inside, which is the real boss.
- A dragon boss collapses, and the corruption driving it erupts as a free-floating Malice entity that must be destroyed before it can re-enter the dragon.

Best for: Final bosses, major villain reveals, the campaign's climax.

**Combination**
Many bosses use elements of multiple transition types, a cosmetic change combined with one environmental shift, for example. This is the most dynamic option and works well for bosses with three or more phases.

> **Transition narration matters.** A phase transition is a cut-scene moment in a video game. Give it the same weight at the table. Describe what happens. Slow down. Let the players react. *"The creature's eyes all close at once. The amber light goes dark. You hear a sound like roots tearing, and then the floor of the chamber cracks open."*

---

## Designing the Arena

The boss chamber is not just a backdrop. It is a participant in the fight.

When designing the arena, ask:

**What does the boss's anatomy demand?**
A flying boss needs vertical space. A charging boss needs a long approach lane. A boss that burrows needs a floor that can be disrupted.

**What does the dungeon item enable here?**
If the dungeon item is the Hookshot, the arena should have hookshot targets: ceiling rings, metal posts, distant platforms. If it's the Boomerang, there should be objects that can be hit or knocked at range. The arena and the item should feel designed for each other.

**What hazard exists to raise the stakes?**
A pit of spikes. Lava channels the boss can knock players into. Pressure-activated traps on the floor. Moving platforms that shift when the boss strikes them. Hazards make the fight three-dimensional. Players are managing position, not just HP.

**What can change?**
Good arenas have dynamic elements that can shift during the fight, often at phase transitions. Water level. Platform configuration. Light sources. Destructible cover. The arena at the end of the fight should feel different from the arena at the beginning.

{{footnote DM Guide | Boss Design }}

{{pageNumber,auto}}

\page
