{{pageNumber,auto}}

\page

> **On The Depths:** Gloom exposure is tracked differently from standard heat and cold. It is a corruption mechanic rather than a temperature one. However, the sustained psychological and physical strain of traveling in total darkness with active Gloom justifies Weather Exhaustion checks for extended travel. DMs may also handle Gloom exposure as its own parallel condition if preferred.

## Adjusting for Story

The table above provides a baseline. The following situations are all valid reasons to depart from it:

**Milder than normal:** *An unusually warm winter in Hebra, a cool wet summer in the Gerudo Desert, a break in the ash cloud over Death Mountain.* Reduce severity by one tier. A party who has worked to earn good weather (lifting a curse, completing a sage quest, restoring a regional spirit) might find conditions easier than expected. That is a reward.

**More severe than normal:** *Calamity weather, Malice-warped storms, divine punishment.* Increase severity by one or two tiers. Increase check frequency. Add secondary effects beyond standard Weather Exhaustion, forced navigation checks, equipment damage, visibility penalties that affect combat.

**Persistent unusual weather:** A blizzard that should last a day keeps going for three. The desert heat isn't letting up as the party crosses deeper in. Don't feel bound by realistic weather cycles if a prolonged environmental threat serves the story better.

**Localized zones:** A single room in a dungeon might have extreme cold (an ice-sealed chamber) without the rest of the dungeon being cold at all. Apply Weather Exhaustion to the room only. Short durations at high DC are more dramatic than long durations at low DC.

---

## Travel Pace and Weather

How fast a party moves through a weather event affects how often checks occur.

| Travel Pace | Effect on Check Frequency |
|:--|:--|
| **Slow pace** | Extend time between checks by 50% (e.g., every 6 hours becomes every 9 hours) |
| **Normal pace** | Use the standard frequency from the table |
| **Fast pace** | Shorten time between checks by 50% (e.g., every 6 hours becomes every 3 hours) |
| **Forced march (8+ hours)** | Treat as one severity tier higher; checks begin immediately on entering the environment |

Slow pace means the party is moving carefully, resting frequently, and managing their exposure. Fast pace means they are pushing through, and the environment punishes that.

\column

## Reading and Forecasting Weather: Player Checks

When a player asks *"How's the weather looking?"*, *"Is it safe to cross the mountain today?"*, or *"Can we make it to the other side of the desert before things get bad?"*, that is a cue to ask for an ability check.

**The check:** Wisdom (Survival) or Intelligence (Nature), DM's choice based on framing. Survival reflects instinct and field experience. Nature reflects academic or studied knowledge of environments.

**The DC depends on how obvious the threat is:**

| Condition Visibility | DC | Examples |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Unmistakable | DC 5 | Tornado visible on the horizon, active volcanic eruption, hurricane-force winds already blowing |
| Obvious | DC 8 | Heavy black storm clouds building over Death Mountain, whiteout conditions beginning, sandstorm dust wall visible in the distance |
| Noticeable | DC 12 | A blizzard vs. a heavy snowstorm — the signs are there, but require experience to read correctly |
| Subtle | DC 15 | Pressure drop before a desert storm, unusual bird behavior before a tornado, specific cloud formations indicating extreme cold inbound |
| Expert-level | DC 18 | Reading Malice weather patterns, predicting Gloom surges in the Depths, identifying magically-induced weather |

**On a success:** Give useful, actionable information. *"The ash cloud over the mountain is moving faster than normal. If you try to cross by the upper trail today, you'll be in it before midday. The lower trail adds two hours but keeps you below the cloud line."*

**On a failure:** The player cannot confidently read the conditions. You are not obligated to deceive them; a failure simply means they do not have enough information to make a certain call. *"The sky looks threatening, but you can't tell if this is the kind of storm that blows over in an hour or the kind that settles in for days."*

> **DM note:** Never punish a player for asking about weather. This is exactly the kind of preparation the system is designed to reward. A player who thinks to ask before crossing Death Mountain is engaging with the world correctly, give them something useful to work with.

{{footnote DM Guide | Weather }}

{{pageNumber,auto}}

\page

## Narrative Hints: Describing the Weather

For **Severe** conditions and above, describe the weather before calling for any check. Players should feel the environment before they are asked to roll against it.

The goal is to build the scene, not to telegraph a mechanical outcome. Describe what the characters experience, what they see, hear, feel, and smell, and let the danger be implied by the description.

**Examples by severity:**

*Moderate:*
> *"The sun has been relentless today, no clouds, no shade along this stretch of field, and the air sits hot and heavy. Your armor is warm to the touch. By afternoon, everyone is drinking more than they planned."*

*Severe:*
> *"The sandstorm moved in faster than you expected. Visibility has dropped to thirty feet, maybe less. Sand finds its way into everything: your eyes, your mouth, the seams of your armor. The wind pushes against you with real force. Shouting to each other is difficult. You can still move, but not easily, and not without cost."*

*Extreme:*
> *"The temperature on the upper slopes of Death Mountain has become something else entirely. The air shimmers with heat you can see. Every breath feels like drawing in from an oven. The rock beneath your boots is too hot to touch with bare hands. Your waterskin is already warm. You are not in danger yet, but you can feel that the mountain does not intend for you to be here."*

*Natural Disaster:*
> *"The tornado is already down. You can see it, a churning column of black and brown cutting across the plain to the southeast, maybe a mile out. The air pressure has changed. Loose debris is moving. Livestock in the distance are running. This is not something you need to assess. This is something you need to decide about right now."*

> **When to narrate vs. when to roll:** Describe the environment freely and frequently. Call for a Weather Exhaustion check only when the defined time interval has elapsed. Do not call for checks mid-description, let the scene land first, then ask for the save at the appropriate moment.


## Quick Adjudication Reference

Use this when you need a fast ruling mid-session without returning to the full tables.

**Is this a Weather Exhaustion situation?**
- Would this kill an unprepared person within a day? → **Yes**
- Does crossing this terrain cost roughly twice normal effort? → **Yes**
- Is this merely miserable, wet, or cold? → **Probably not**

**What DC and frequency?**
- Rough conditions, wrong gear, long exposure → **DC 8 / 12 hours**
- Serious threat, minimal protection → **DC 10 / 6 hours**
- Dangerous environment, even with preparation → **DC 12 / 3 hours**
- Actively life-threatening, immediate danger → **DC 16 / 1 hour**

**What reduces or eliminates checks?**
- Appropriate armor set for the environment → Advantage on checks, or remove one severity tier
- Appropriate elixir (Chilly, Spicy, Fireproof) → Advantage on checks for 30 minutes
- Racial resistance (Goron fire resistance, Rito cold tolerance) → Advantage
- Racial immunity → Automatic success
- Shelter (cave, tent, magical space) → Checks suspended for the duration

{{footnote DM Guide | Weather }}

{{pageNumber,auto}}

\page

# Hyrule Factions & NPCs

> *"Hyrule is not one kingdom. It is a hundred small kingdoms that have agreed, for now, to call themselves one."*
> — Viator Fortuitus, A Bard's Record

A region only feels alive when the people in it want things, when factions have agendas that exist independently of the player characters, when helping one group has consequences with another, and when NPCs feel like they have lives that continue whether or not the party is watching.

This chapter gives you the tools to bring Hyrule's political landscape to the table: profiles for eleven major factions, a framework for handling inter-faction relationships and the consequences of player choices, five sample NPCs ready to drop into any campaign, and adventure hooks to get you started immediately.

---

## Using This Chapter Across Different Timelines

Hyrule's political landscape shifts dramatically depending on when your campaign is set. The Royal Family's power, the Yiga Clan's strength, the state of Zora-Goron relations, all of it depends on your campaign's era and tone.

This chapter is written as a **modular framework**, not a fixed snapshot. Each faction profile gives you the *underlying motivations and tensions* that tend to hold true across eras, plus guidance on how those motivations might shift depending on your campaign's timeline. Before you run a session involving a faction, decide:

- **Is the Royal Family currently in power, displaced, or absent?** This affects nearly every other faction's posture.
- **Has a Calamity (or Calamity-equivalent threat) recently occurred, is one ongoing, or is the world in a period of peace?** Factions behave very differently during active crisis versus long-term stability.
- **How much time has passed since the last major conflict?** Old grudges soften or harden depending on how recent they are.

Once you've answered these questions for your campaign, apply that context to every faction below. A faction profile that says "currently allied with the Crown" might mean something very different in a campaign where the Crown has fallen.

\column
## Major Factions of Hyrule

### The Royal Family of Hyrule

**What They Want:** Stability above all else. The Royal Family's central concern is the continuity of the kingdom, maintaining order, preventing a recurrence of past Calamities, and preserving the bloodline's connection to Hylia's blessing. Individual members of the family may have more personal agendas (a prince seeking to prove himself, a princess pursuing forbidden research into ancient magic), but the institution itself wants Hyrule to endure.

**What They Fear:** The return of a great evil. Internal rebellion or loss of legitimacy. The bloodline's sacred power failing to manifest in an heir. Losing the loyalty of allied races.

**What Quests They Give:** Investigate disturbances threatening the kingdom's stability. Escort or protect members of the nobility. Recover lost relics tied to the bloodline's power. Mediate disputes between allied races that threaten the kingdom's unity. Investigate corruption within the castle itself.

**If Players Help Them:** Access to royal resources: funding, equipment, introductions to nobility, legitimacy that opens doors elsewhere. The party may be granted titles, land, or formal recognition.

**If Players Oppose Them:** The Royal Guard and allied forces become obstacles. Other factions loyal to the Crown may treat the party with suspicion. However, factions with grievances against the Crown (Yiga Clan, disenfranchised groups) may see the party as potential allies.

{{footnote DM Guide | Factions }}

{{pageNumber,auto}}

\page

### The Sheikah

**What They Want:** The protection of the Royal Family and the preservation of ancient knowledge, including knowledge dangerous enough that it must be guarded rather than shared. Sheikah are bound by ancient oath to Hylia's bloodline, and that duty defines almost everything they do.

**What They Fear:** A repeat of the betrayal that birthed the Yiga Clan. The loss or misuse of ancient technology under their care. The Royal Family falling, leaving their oath without a clear purpose.

**What Quests They Give:** Investigate threats to the Royal Family before they manifest. Recover or secure ancient Sheikah technology that has fallen into the wrong hands. Escort scholars to dangerous ruins. Eliminate specific threats quietly, without drawing public attention.

**If Players Help Them:** Access to ancient technology, training in stealth and precision combat, introductions to a network of watchers and informants across Hyrule. Sheikah trust is hard-won but extremely valuable once earned.

**If Players Oppose Them:** The Sheikah do not forget, and they do not forgive easily. Expect to be watched, followed, and eventually confronted: quietly, precisely, and without warning.

---

### The Yiga Clan

**What They Want:** Vengeance against the Sheikah and the Royal Family for a betrayal in their shared past, and devotion to Ganon (or an equivalent Calamity figure) as the only power they believe can topple the old order. Individual Yiga may have more personal motivations, many genuinely believe they are righting an ancient wrong.

**What They Fear:** The Sheikah have wisdom and resources the Yiga abandoned when they split off. The Yiga's chosen patron failing or being defeated removes their entire purpose. Internal betrayal, having broken from the Sheikah once, the Yiga are acutely aware that it could happen to them too.

**What Quests They Give:** (Less common as conventional quest-givers, but possible) Retrieve a sacred Yiga relic. Eliminate a Sheikah target the Yiga consider a traitor to their original cause. Some disillusioned Yiga may seek to defect and need protection.

**If Players Help Them:** This is a significant moral choice. The Yiga may offer dangerous power, forbidden techniques, or simply safe passage through their territory. Other factions (Sheikah especially) will become hostile.

**If Players Oppose Them:** The default state for most heroic campaigns. The Yiga become recurring antagonists, banana-obsessed comic relief on the surface, genuinely dangerous assassins underneath.

---

### The Gerudo Tribes

**What They Want:** Survival and prosperity for their people in a harsh desert environment, autonomy from outside interference, and (depending on era) opportunities for Gerudo to participate more fully in wider Hyrulean society, trade, diplomacy, even succession to leadership roles historically denied to them.

**What They Fear:** Resource scarcity (especially water). External powers attempting to control Gerudo Desert's resources or strategic position. The recurrence of conflict tied to historical figures who emerged from Gerudo society and turned against Hyrule.

**What Quests They Give:** Escort caravans through dangerous desert terrain. Investigate threats to Gerudo Fortress or trade routes. Negotiate trade or political agreements with other kingdoms. Recover stolen artifacts or sacred items.

**If Players Help Them:** Trade access, training in desert survival and Gerudo combat techniques, political goodwill that matters significantly if the party later needs Gerudo military or economic support.

**If Players Oppose Them:** The Gerudo are proud and do not easily forget insult, but they are pragmatic: a faction that values strength may respect a worthy opponent even while opposing them.

---

### Zora's Domain

**What They Want:** The preservation of their waterways, their traditions, and their independence. Many Zora communities place enormous value on craftsmanship, artistry, and the maintenance of ancient agreements (marriage alliances, water rights, sacred springs) with neighboring peoples.

**What They Fear:** Pollution or disruption of their water sources. The breaking of ancient pacts. Outsiders failing to respect Zora customs (a notoriously sensitive issue around royal marriage customs in many eras).

**What Quests They Give:** Investigate threats to water quality or supply. Recover items lost in deep or dangerous waters. Mediate disputes with upstream neighbors (see the Zora/Goron tension example below). Escort important figures through dangerous waters.

**If Players Help Them:** Access to Zora armor and aquatic technology, safe passage and assistance in all Zora waterways, a powerful ally in any conflict involving water-based threats.

**If Players Oppose Them:** Zora's Domain can effectively seal itself off, denying access to the party. Downstream settlements that depend on Zora goodwill for water access may suffer, and notice who is responsible.

{{footnote DM Guide | Factions }}

{{pageNumber,auto}}

\page

### Goron City

**What They Want:** Stability of their mountain home, continued access to the minerals and ore that sustain their economy and craft, and the wellbeing of their community. Gorons place enormous value on communal celebration, hospitality, and strength used in service of others.

**What They Fear:** Volcanic instability that threatens the mountain itself. Resource depletion. Conflicts that disrupt their famously warm relationships with neighboring peoples (Gorons generally try to get along with everyone, which makes conflict especially painful for them).

**What Quests They Give:** Clear dangerous creatures from mining tunnels. Investigate volcanic instability or unusual seismic activity. Deliver goods or messages across dangerous mountain terrain. Resolve disputes over mining practices (see below).

**If Players Help Them:** Access to Goron-forged weapons and armor, fire resistance training, an extremely loyal ally. Gorons who consider you family will go to great lengths for you.

**If Players Oppose Them:** Difficult, since Gorons are slow to anger, but if pushed, their raw strength makes them formidable, and their extended community means word travels fast.

---

### Rito Village

**What They Want:** Protection of their mountain and coastal territories, mastery and preservation of their aerial traditions, and (in many eras) careful balance between tradition and adaptation as the wider world changes around them.

**What They Fear:** Threats from the sky: storms, aerial predators, hostile flying enemies. Loss of their territories to encroachment. The erosion of Rito tradition and flying culture.

**What Quests They Give:** Investigate aerial threats or disappearances. Deliver messages or items across long distances via flight (for non-Rito parties, this becomes "escort the Rito messenger"). Recover items lost to height or storms. Defend against threats to their village.

**If Players Help Them:** Rito goodwill grants access to aerial scouting, fast information networks (Rito messengers travel far and fast), and an ally with unmatched aerial combat capability.

**If Players Oppose Them:** Rito are proud and direct: expect confrontation rather than scheming, but also expect it to be swift and decisive given their aerial advantage.

\column

### Zonai Researchers

**What They Want:** Understanding and preservation of ancient Zonai technology and knowledge, often balanced against an awareness that such technology can be catastrophically dangerous if misused. Depending on your campaign's framing, Zonai Researchers might be actual Zonai descendants, or scholars (of any race) devoted to studying Zonai ruins and artifacts.

**What They Fear:** Ancient technology falling into reckless or malicious hands. The loss of irreplaceable knowledge through careless excavation or destruction. Their research being suppressed or weaponized by political powers.

**What Quests They Give:** Explore dangerous ruins to recover or document Zonai technology. Protect research sites from looters or hostile creatures. Investigate malfunctioning ancient constructs. Decode ancient texts or mechanisms.

**If Players Help Them:** Access to Zonai-tech equipment, schematics, and constructs. Knowledge of ancient Hyrule's history that may be relevant to the campaign's larger mysteries.

**If Players Oppose Them:** Relatively low-stakes as direct antagonists (most are scholars, not warriors), but their constructs and automated defenses can be quite dangerous, and they may withhold critical information the party needs.

---

### Deku Groves

**What They Want:** The protection and health of their forest territories, autonomy from outside interference, and (for individual Deku) a complicated mix of genuine community loyalty and entrepreneurial self-interest. Deku society values both deeply.

**What They Fear:** Deforestation, fire, and other threats to their groves. Corruption of the forest's natural magic. Outsiders who do not respect forest boundaries and customs.

**What Quests They Give:** Clear threats to a grove's health (corrupted plants, invasive creatures). Deliver or retrieve goods through dangerous forest terrain. Resolve trade disputes (Business Scrubs are notoriously sharp dealers). Investigate disturbances in ancient, sacred parts of the forest.

**If Players Help Them:** Safe passage through Deku territory (otherwise notoriously difficult to navigate), access to unique forest goods and nature magic, goodwill from a typically insular people.

**If Players Oppose Them:** Deku groves can become hostile, hidden mazes; the forest itself seems to work against intruders. Trade access is cut off.

{{footnote DM Guide | Factions }}

{{pageNumber,auto}}

\page

### The Twili

**What They Want:** Depends enormously on your campaign's framing of the Twilight Realm. Commonly: maintaining the boundary between the Twilight Realm and the Light World, understanding or escaping their exile (if your lore includes a banishment), and protecting their own realm from threats, including threats that might try to use the Twilight Realm as a weapon against Hyrule.

**What They Fear:** The boundary between realms collapsing uncontrolled. Their own history of exile and what caused it repeating. Being misunderstood or treated as inherently hostile by Light World peoples (a real risk, given their unsettling appearance to outsiders).

**What Quests They Give:** Investigate breaches between the Twilight Realm and the Light World. Recover items or individuals lost between realms. Address corrupting influences that threaten both realms. Mediate growing tension between Twili and Light World peoples.

**If Players Help Them:** Access to twilight magic, safe passage through the Twilight Realm, an ally with unique insight into shadow and illusion-based threats.

**If Players Oppose Them:** The Twili can be a genuinely unsettling antagonist faction, not evil, but alien enough that conflict with them feels existentially different from conflict with other Hyrulean peoples.

\column

### Bandits, Pirates & Outlaw Groups

**What They Want:** Varies enormously by group: survival, wealth, freedom from a society that has failed or exploited them, or simple opportunism. Some outlaw groups are genuinely villainous; others are desperate people failed by the systems meant to protect them; others are romanticized folk-hero figures (a "noble bandit" archetype is common in Hyrule's storytelling tradition).

**What They Fear:** Capture and Royal justice. Rival outlaw groups encroaching on territory. Running out of resources or safe havens.

**What Quests They Give:** (As antagonists) Defend a settlement from raids. Recover stolen goods. (As potential allies or quest-givers) Smuggle goods or people past authorities. Investigate corruption that outlaws claim drove them to crime.

**If Players Help Them:** Access to black-market goods, information networks that operate outside official channels, and morally complex storytelling opportunities.

**If Players Oppose Them:** Standard heroic conflict, though consider whether your particular outlaw group deserves a purely villainous treatment or a more nuanced one.

{{footnote DM Guide | Factions }}

{{pageNumber,auto}}

\page

## Faction Relationships

Factions in Hyrule do not exist in isolation. Their relationships with each other create some of the richest adventure material available to a DM, particularly when player choices force them to take a side, broker peace, or live with the consequences of remaining neutral.

### The Relationship Web

Rather than a fixed chart (which would not survive contact with your specific campaign), think of faction relationships along these axes for any two factions you want to connect:

**Resource Tension:** Do these factions compete for or depend on the same resource? (Water, land, trade routes, ore, magic.)

**Historical Grievance:** Is there a past conflict, betrayal, or unresolved tension between them? (The Sheikah/Yiga split is the clearest example, but smaller historical tensions can exist between any two peoples.)

**Ideological Difference:** Do they fundamentally disagree about how Hyrule should be governed, how outsiders should be treated, or how tradition versus progress should be balanced?

**Mutual Dependency:** Do they need each other despite tension? (A desert tribe that needs water from a river kingdom, a mountain people that trades ore for food they cannot grow.)

### Worked Example: The Zora–Goron Tributary Dispute

This example shows how a faction relationship becomes a playable adventure scenario.

**The Situation:** Goron City's mining operations have intensified, and runoff from their ore processing has begun polluting a tributary river that flows down into Zora territory. The water isn't poisoned exactly, but it's increasingly cloudy, mineral-heavy, and harmful to the fish populations Zora communities depend on. Zora elders have sent formal complaints. Goron leadership is sympathetic but points out that the mining supports hundreds of families and any slowdown threatens their economy.

**Why This Works as an Adventure:** Neither side is purely right or wrong. Both have legitimate needs. There is no single "correct" answer, which means player choices genuinely matter.

**Possible Player Approaches:**

- **Broker a technical compromise.** Help the Gorons develop better filtration or processing methods (perhaps requiring a quest to recover ancient Zonai filtration technology, or consulting with a Zonai Researcher). This is the "everybody wins" path but requires the most effort and may take multiple sessions.
- **Support the Zora.** Pressure the Gorons to halt or reduce mining. This protects Zora interests but damages Goron goodwill and potentially their economy. Goron quest-givers may become less friendly, and the local mining community may resent the party.
- **Support the Gorons.** Argue that the mining is too economically vital to halt, perhaps offering the Zora compensation or assistance adapting to the changed river. This protects Goron interests but damages Zora trust, fishing communities downstream may directly blame the party.
- **Find a third path.** Players might propose relocating the affected Zora communities, discover an alternate water source, or uncover that a third party (Yiga sabotage, a corrupted spirit, a Zonai construct malfunction) is actually worsening the pollution beyond what normal mining would cause, turning a political dispute into a more conventional adventure hook.
- **Do nothing.** A valid choice with consequences: the dispute escalates, potentially into actual conflict between Zora and Goron settlements, and the party's inaction becomes a notable fact NPCs remember.

**Consequences to Track:** Whichever path the party takes, note it. Goron and Zora NPCs encountered later should reflect what happened. If the party sided with the Gorons, Zora NPCs may be cold or pointed in conversation. If the party found the clever third-path solution, both factions might speak well of the party to others, building a reputation that opens doors elsewhere.

> **DM Tip:** This template (two factions with legitimate competing needs, several possible resolutions, and lasting consequences) can be reused with any pair of factions. Try: Gerudo water rights vs. a Hylian settlement, Rito territorial claims vs. Zonai Researcher excavation sites, Deku grove boundaries vs. a logging operation supplying a Hylian town.

{{footnote DM Guide | Factions }}

{{pageNumber,auto}}

\page

## Sample NPCs

Five NPCs, one drawn from a different major faction, ready to use immediately. Each includes roleplaying notes; combat stats are included only where the NPC is realistically likely to fight.

---

### Lira Stonewatch: Sheikah Information Broker

**Faction:** The Sheikah
**Role:** Information broker and unofficial liaison between the Sheikah and outsiders the Sheikah have deemed useful

**Appearance:** Pale ash-toned skin, sharp crimson eyes, dressed in unremarkable traveling clothes that deliberately avoid any Sheikah iconography. Carries a simple walking stick that is, in fact, a finely balanced weapon.

**Personality:** Lira speaks carefully, in complete sentences, never wasting words. She has a dry sense of humor she rarely shows, and seems to find most people's impatience quietly amusing. She is not unfriendly, simply economical.

**Voice/Mannerism:** Speaks slowly and evenly. Often pauses before answering questions, as if weighing exactly how much truth a person has earned. Maintains steady, slightly unnerving eye contact.

**Motivation:** Lira gathers information across Hyrule on behalf of the Sheikah, and occasionally shares pieces of it with adventurers whose goals happen to align with Sheikah interests. She is not an ally exactly, more a transactional acquaintance who finds the party useful.

**Roleplaying Notes:** Lira always knows more than she shares. She will trade information for information, favors for favors, and rarely gives anything away for free, though she occasionally makes exceptions for parties who have proven trustworthy. If pressed about Sheikah secrets, she deflects smoothly without ever quite lying.

**Combat Capability:** Lira is a trained Sheikah operative. If forced to fight, use the **Veilblade** class features at character level 6, or a custom stat block with Stealth +9, Dexterity-based attacks, and the ability to vanish using Sheikah shadow techniques (treat as a 2nd-level Invisibility spell, usable once per short rest).

**Adventure Hooks:**
1. Lira approaches the party with information about a threat the Sheikah have noticed but cannot openly investigate without drawing attention. She needs deniable agents.
2. The party discovers Lira has been feeding them selectively true information for her own purposes, and must decide whether to confront her, work around her, or accept the arrangement as the price of useful intelligence.

\column

### Kass Windrender: Rito Wandering Bard

**Faction:** Rito Village (semi-independent)
**Role:** Traveling musician and unofficial chronicler of Hyrule's current events

**Appearance:** A Rito with striking blue-gray plumage, carrying a well-worn accordion-like instrument decorated with feathers from places he's visited. Travels light and far.

**Personality:** Warm, curious, and endlessly delighted by stories. Kass has no particular agenda beyond seeing the world and turning what he finds into song. He is gossipy in the best sense, eager to share what he knows and equally eager to hear what the party knows.

**Voice/Mannerism:** Speaks musically, sometimes literally breaking into song mid-conversation. Asks a lot of questions. Genuinely listens to the answers.

**Motivation:** Kass travels Hyrule documenting its history, its heroes, and its changes through music. He has an uncanny way of showing up wherever something significant is happening.

**Roleplaying Notes:** Kass is an excellent recurring NPC. He can appear in any region, has heard rumors about almost anything happening in the wider world, and will happily trade information for a good story. He's not a combatant and should generally avoid danger, fleeing or hiding rather than fighting.

**Combat Capability:** None significant. Kass avoids combat entirely. If endangered, he relies on his flight speed (Rito base 30 ft. flying speed) to escape.

**Adventure Hooks:**
1. Kass has heard a song fragment, an old riddle-rhyme, that seems to point toward the location of something the party needs (a relic, a lost dungeon, a sage's hiding place), but he doesn't know what it means.
2. Kass asks the party for their story so far, in exchange for sharing useful regional rumors, giving the DM a natural opportunity to recap and seed future hooks.

{{footnote DM Guide | Factions }}

{{pageNumber,auto}}

\page

### Sela Stormsand: Gerudo Caravan Captain

**Faction:** Gerudo Tribes
**Role:** Leader of a trading caravan operating between Gerudo Desert and Hyrule Field

**Appearance:** Tall, imposing, with the traditional Gerudo build and striking red hair tied back for desert travel. Wears practical desert gear modified for combat readiness. This is a woman who has fought off bandits more than once.

**Personality:** Direct, confident, and protective of her people, both her caravan crew and the Gerudo more broadly. She has little patience for outsiders who treat Gerudo with suspicion or condescension, but is warm and generous to those who earn her respect.

**Voice/Mannerism:** Speaks bluntly, often with a hint of challenge in her tone. She is testing people, even in casual conversation. Laughs loudly and genuinely when something actually amuses her.

**Motivation:** Sela's caravan is the economic lifeline for several smaller Gerudo settlements. She is fiercely committed to keeping trade routes safe and profitable, and views threats to her caravan as threats to her people's survival.

**Roleplaying Notes:** Sela respects strength and competence above almost everything else. She will test the party, perhaps with a blunt question, a minor challenge, or simply by watching how they handle themselves, before deciding whether to trust them. Once earned, her loyalty is considerable.

**Combat Capability:** Sela is a capable warrior. Use Champion class features at character level 5, or a custom stat block: AC 16, HP 58, Scimitar attacks +7 to hit (1d6+4 slashing), proficient in Athletics and Intimidation.

**Adventure Hooks:**
1. Sela's caravan has been targeted by bandits with suspiciously good information about her routes and schedule. She suspects an inside leak and wants discreet help investigating.
2. Sela offers the party passage and protection across the desert in exchange for help recovering cargo lost to a sandstorm (or stolen by Yiga raiders), a straightforward but tone-setting introduction to Gerudo territory.

\column

### Dento: Zora Royal Goldsmith

**Faction:** Zora's Domain
**Role:** Master craftsman responsible for ceremonial and royal Zora jewelry and armor pieces

**Appearance:** An elderly Zora with weathered, pale-blue scales and ornate jewelry of his own making. Moves slowly but with obvious dignity.

**Personality:** Painstaking, proud of his craft, and deeply traditional. Dento takes his work as a sacred duty rather than mere trade, and speaks about craftsmanship with genuine reverence.

**Voice/Mannerism:** Formal, precise speech. Often pauses mid-sentence to examine something (a piece of jewelry, a stranger's equipment, the quality of a blade) with genuine professional interest.

**Motivation:** Dento wants to preserve Zora craftsmanship traditions and ensure his knowledge passes to a worthy successor. He is also quietly worried about sourcing rare materials as certain mining and trade relationships have grown strained (a hook that ties naturally to the Zora-Goron tension example above).

**Roleplaying Notes:** Dento is an excellent source for magic item lore, identification services, and crafting-related quests. He is slow to trust outsiders with sensitive commissions but extremely loyal once a relationship is established.

**Combat Capability:** None. Dento is an elderly craftsman with no combat training. He relies entirely on Zora Domain guards for protection.

**Adventure Hooks:**
1. Dento needs a rare material, found only in a dangerous location, to complete a ceremonial piece for an upcoming royal occasion, and is willing to pay handsomely (or trade a custom-crafted item) for its retrieval.
2. Dento suspects one of his apprentices has been selling design secrets to outside parties and wants the party to investigate quietly, without damaging the reputation of his workshop.

{{footnote DM Guide | Factions }}

{{pageNumber,auto}}

\page

### Mara: Reformed Yiga Defector

**Faction:** Formerly Yiga Clan; currently unaffiliated
**Role:** A former Yiga foot soldier who has abandoned the Clan and is trying to build a new life under an assumed identity

**Appearance:** Unremarkable on purpose. Mara has deliberately styled herself to avoid any resemblance to her former life, wearing simple, practical clothes and keeping her banana-print sash carefully hidden away as the only memento she couldn't bring herself to discard.

**Personality:** Guarded, anxious, and quietly desperate for a normal life. Mara left the Yiga after growing disillusioned with the Clan's violence, but she carries guilt over her past actions and fear of being discovered.

**Voice/Mannerism:** Speaks quietly, rarely makes eye contact for long, and startles easily at sudden movements or loud noises. Becomes noticeably more confident and direct when discussing combat or Yiga tactics, old training shows through.

**Motivation:** Mara wants to disappear, build a new identity, and atone in whatever small ways she can for her past. She is terrified of Yiga retribution for her defection.

**Roleplaying Notes:** Mara is a morally complex NPC: sympathetic, but with a genuinely violent past the party may eventually learn about. She is a good source of inside knowledge about Yiga tactics, hideouts, and members, but sharing this information terrifies her and she'll only do so if she trusts the party significantly.

**Combat Capability:** Mara retains her Yiga training. Use Veilblade or Masked Wanderer class features at character level 4, or a custom stat block: AC 15, HP 38, Dual dagger attacks +6 to hit (1d4+3 piercing each), proficient in Stealth and Acrobatics. She avoids combat when possible and fights defensively if cornered.

**Adventure Hooks:**
1. Yiga Clan members have picked up Mara's trail, and she pleads with the party for protection, drawing them into direct conflict with the Clan as a side effect of an act of kindness.
2. Mara possesses specific knowledge of a Yiga hideout or operation that could help the party with an unrelated quest, but giving up this information means risking her own exposure and safety.

\column

## Quick-Use Faction Adventure Hook Index

For fast reference, here are the adventure hooks listed by faction (minimum two each, drawing from both the faction profiles and the relationship example above).

| Faction | Hook 1 | Hook 2 |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Royal Family** | Investigate a disturbance threatening the kingdom's stability | Protect a member of the nobility during a dangerous journey |
| **Sheikah** | Recover ancient technology that has fallen into the wrong hands | Quietly eliminate a threat to the Royal Family without public exposure |
| **Yiga Clan** | A disillusioned Yiga member seeks to defect and needs protection | Investigate (or interfere with) a Yiga plot against the Crown |
| **Gerudo Tribes** | Escort a caravan through dangerous desert terrain | Investigate a leak compromising Gerudo trade route security |
| **Zora's Domain** | Resolve the tributary pollution dispute with Goron City | Recover an item lost in dangerous waters |
| **Goron City** | Clear dangerous creatures from a mining tunnel | Investigate unusual seismic activity threatening the mountain |
| **Rito Village** | Investigate an aerial threat to the village's territory | Deliver a critical message across long, dangerous distance |
| **Zonai Researchers** | Protect a research site from looters or hostile creatures | Investigate a malfunctioning ancient construct |
| **Deku Groves** | Clear a corruption threatening a sacred grove | Resolve a trade dispute with a sharp-dealing Business Scrub |
| **Twili** | Investigate a breach between the Twilight Realm and Light World | Mediate rising tension between Twili and a Light World settlement |
| **Bandits/Outlaws** | Defend a settlement from an outlaw raid | Investigate whether an outlaw group's claims of being failed by the system have merit |

# Appendix A: Conditions

The 2014 Player's Handbook conditions (blinded, charmed, deafened, frightened, grappled, incapacitated, invisible, paralyzed, petrified, poisoned, prone, restrained, stunned, unconscious, exhaustion) work exactly as written and are not reprinted here.

This appendix collects the conditions and tracked states that are **original to Zelda DnD**, which were previously defined only in the chapters that introduced them.

---

### Weather Exhaustion
*(Temperature)*

A separate track from standard exhaustion, gained by failing a Weather Exhaustion check in extreme heat, extreme cold, or a storm. **It has four levels and cannot kill you.**

| Level | Effect |
|:--:|:--|
| 1 | Disadvantage on **Perception checks** and **initiative rolls** |
| 2 | Disadvantage on **all ability checks** |
| 3 | Speed reduced by **10 feet**. At the start of each of your turns, choose attack rolls or saving throws; you have disadvantage on the chosen rolls until the start of your next turn |
| 4 | Speed reduced by **20 feet**, and you **cannot gain advantage** on any d20 roll |

**At level 4, a further failed check gives you 1 level of standard exhaustion instead.** That is the only way Weather Exhaustion can lead to death, and it happens through the standard track rather than this one.

Weather Exhaustion is reduced by **1 level per short or long rest**, provided you are sheltered from the environment that caused it. It is a separate condition from standard exhaustion; effects that remove one do not remove the other unless they say so.

---

### Arcane Saturation
*(Magic System)*

Gained by casting spells that cost 5 MP or more. Tracked openly by the player.

| Level | Effect |
|:--:|:--|
| 1 | No effect |
| 2 | Arcane Strain costs an additional +25% |
| 3 | Disadvantage on spell attack rolls |
| 4 | Spell save DCs reduced by 1 |
| 5+ | You cannot cast spells costing 5 MP or more |

Resets at the end of combat, or after one uninterrupted minute without casting.

\column

### Arcane Wounds
*(Magic System)*

Lasting damage to a caster's magical channels, taken by forcing a spell you cannot pay for. Wounds stack and are cumulative. Removed one at a time by a long rest, a Blue Potion, or a Great Fairy.

---

### Marked
*(Ranger)*

A creature designated by Hunter's Insight. The Ranger learns facts about it and several Ranger features key off it. A creature can be Marked by only one Ranger at a time.

---

### Elemental Marks
*(Shaman)*

Flame, Frost, Storm and Root Marks applied by Shaman spells. Applying a second Mark to a marked creature triggers an **Elemental Reaction** instead of stacking. Marks last until the end of the Shaman's next turn, or their second following turn from 9th level.

---

### Swallowed
*(Enemies, Bosses)*

A creature swallowed by a larger creature is **blinded and restrained**, has total cover against attacks from outside, and takes the damage listed in the swallowing creature's stat block at the start of each of its turns. It escapes by dealing the listed damage from inside, or when the swallower dies.

---

### Bleeding
*(Veilblade)*

The creature takes the listed damage at the start of each of its turns. Bleeding does not stack; a second application extends the duration or increases the die as the feature says, and nothing else. Ended by any healing.

---

### Dazed
*(Veilblade, Called Shots)*

The creature has disadvantage on its next attack roll. Dazed does not stack. A second application while already dazed generally upgrades to stunned; see the effect that applied it.

---

### Perfect Parry
*(Items)*

Not a condition but a trigger: a parry with a shield that reduces the incoming damage to 0. Some shields and relics key extra effects off one.

{{footnote Appendices | Conditions }}

# Appendix B: Advancement

This book uses the standard 2014 advancement rules. What follows is guidance on running them in Hyrule, and the one thing this book adds.

---

## Milestone or Experience

**Milestone advancement is recommended for this setting,** and it is what the dungeon and boss chapters assume. A Zelda story is shaped like a series of places, and the natural moment to level is when the party leaves one of them.

**Level up when the party:**

- completes a dungeon and takes what was at the bottom of it,
- resolves a regional arc (a village saved, a faction won over, a corruption cleared),
- or defeats a named boss.

That lands a group at roughly **level 10 after five dungeons** and **level 20 after a full campaign of twelve to fifteen**, which is the pace the enemy chapter is built for.

**If you prefer experience points,** the standard 5e table and the XP values printed in every stat block work without modification. Zelda DnD does not change how XP is earned or how much a level costs.

---

## What a Level Brings

At every level, in this order:

1. **Hit points.** Roll your class's Hit Die, or take the fixed value, and add your Constitution modifier.
2. **Proficiency bonus,** if the class table shows an increase.
3. **Class features** listed on your class table for that level.
4. **SP and MP,** which are columns on the same table. Both increase on their own schedule.
5. **Path or subclass features,** if your path grants one at that level.
6. **Ability Score Improvement,** at the levels your class lists, which you may trade for a feat.

Nothing in this book changes how any of that works. If your class table and this list disagree, the class table is right.

\column

## Tiers of Play in Hyrule

The four tiers of 5e play map cleanly onto the shape of a Zelda story, and knowing which one you are in tells you what relics to hand out.

{{classTable,frame
##### Tiers of Play
| Levels | What the party is | Relic tier | The stakes |
|:--:|:--|:--:|:--|
| **1–4** | Locals with a problem | Tier 4 | A village, a wood, a road |
| **5–10** | Adventurers with a reputation | Tier 4–3 | A region, a people, a temple |
| **11–16** | Champions | Tier 3–2 | The kingdom |
| **17–20** | The chosen | Tier 2–1 | The world, and everything after it |
}}

**The Triforce belongs at 20th, or after it.** Handing out a piece earlier is a legitimate choice, and it will define everything that follows; see **Running the Triforce** in the Relics chapter before you do.

---

## No Multiclassing

**This book does not use multiclassing rules, and that is deliberate.** Five different class resources are in play across the ten classes (Stamina Points, Magic Points, Demonic Power Points, Energy, and Focus Points), and none of them were balanced against being combined. A character in Zelda DnD advances in one class for twenty levels.

If a player wants the feeling of a second calling, the tools are already here:

- **Feats.** Magic Initiate gives a martial real spells. Martial Adept gives a caster real Special Attacks. Both are rewritten in this book to work with its resources.
- **Paths.** Every class's path choice at 3rd level is a bigger identity shift than most multiclass dips.
- **Relics.** A Lesser Relic gives a character a verb no class grants. That is what they are for.
- **Backgrounds.** The thing your character was before is where a second skill set belongs.
